subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, June 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent for an address to His Majesty the King praying that a measure be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom to effect an amendment to the British North America Act with respect to readjustment of the representation in the House of Commons, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefen-baker.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday when the debate was adjourned I was referring to remarks made about the maritime provinces during this debate on redistribution. In particular I was attempting to rectify an erroneous impression that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was speaking in a derogatory vein when he stated the the maritimes needed vision and initiative more than a new system of redistribution in order to cure certain of their ills.
I have no quarrel with the resolution on redistribution. It would appear to be in the best interests of Canada. I cannot, however, support the amendment. Much has been said in a legal vein as to whether or not the federal government can take the action it proposes to take without consulting the provinces, but in the final analysis this house would appear to accept in general the principles set forth in the resolution.
I do not feel that we in the maritimes have any grounds to fear that the proposed plan for redistribution, if adopted, will react against us.
My last remarks before the adjournment yesterday dealt with the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), at page 2478 of Hansard, to the effect that with clearer vision as to this country's future, we in the maritimes can have plants running twelve months a year, and sell our goods to central and western Canada.

I had started before the adjournment yesterday to place before the house the fact that although in many instances we are able to compete on even terms or better with our central Canadian competitors in the production of commodities, we have lost orders because when freight rates are added, the price of our goods laid down in central or western Canada is greater than the price for the same goods manufactured closer to their destination. We most certainly do not lack the vision to recognize this problem. We have realized for years that it is working to our disadvantage, but neither vision nor initiative has altered the situation appreciably. The Minister of Agriculture knows full well that the same conditions are encountered by the western provinces, and British Columbia, in particular, faces problems that are not unlike those we face in the maritimes.
The following statement made bjr the transportation commission of the maritime board of trade crystallizes the disadvantage we are suffering in the maritimes because of our geographical location:
Inasmuch as transportation exerts a tremendous influence upon the location of economic enterprise, it appears that some recent studies on the economy of the maritimes from the postwar viewpoint have failed to give sufficient weight to the effects of the transportation factor in the locational pattern of industry.
The tendency has been for manufacturing to be located close to the markets, away from the raw materials due to the "value of service" principle in railway rate-making, which results in increased charges as fabrication progresses.
If vision is required in solving this problem generally, then I would say to the house that it is vision on a broad Canadian basis, and not vision on the part of the maritime provinces alone. However, when considering our transportation problem, maritimers should not blamd the Minister of Agriculture in any respect. In fact, it was he who was chiefly responsible for the arrangement whereby feed is shipped into the maritimes free of cost, to circumvent this problem of transportation.
The minister suggested that fuller advantage be taken of water routes in bringing our goods to central and western Canada. At page 2478 of Hansard the minister recommended that the maritimes use the water routes by way of Hudson bay and the St. Lawrence river to place their goods on the central Canadian and western markets. It is true that developments in science have brought us to the point where it may now be possible to visualize longer navigation seasons on these two routes, but if we are to take a practical view we must realize that we are still confronted with difficulties, in

Redistribution
that the St, Lawrence river and Hudson bay are inaccessible for many months of the year. I would say that vision and initiative of the magnitude required to make these water routes accessible on a year-round practical basis are not yet available to this generation. Science and other developments simply have not gone that far.
In the maritimes we feel we have the same natural endowments as Canadians elsewhere, and we are just as willing and eager to apply them; but the fact is that to achieve the same results as people in central Canada, it has been and still is necessary for us to bring to bear on the problem a disproportionate amount of vision, initiative, facilities, abilities and so on, to compensate for our geographical location. The alleviation of our disadvantages is a matter of cooperation on a federal or national scale; and it is here that we find ourselves in the ruck, because vision and initiative are not always applied to as great an extent as we in the maritimes sometimes wish. When discussing the matter of lack of vision and initiative we can accuse central Canada, and sometimes the federal government, just as easily and with as much justification as they have for any accusation they direct at us. However, it is not a matter of accusation; it is a case for cooperation. We must regard it as a Canadian and not a regional problem.
I would invite the attention of the house to the June 15 issue of the Financial Post and commend it to readers; it may be that they will get some idea from this issue that we in the maritimes attempt to show some initiative. The article is entitled:
Maritimes Streamline Trade Methods, Modernize Production to Gain Markets
It states in the first two paragraphs:
Maritimers have long ago_ come to learn that their economic well-being hinges largely on the kind of trade agreements Ottawa makes with other world countries and they are perhaps more conscious of that fact to-day than ever. But, with world trade policies still in the making, Nova Scotia. New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island aren't waiting for Ottawa to put them on their post-war feet or otherwise.
They are taking direct action to stimulate trade by producing better quality goods at competitive prices, newr and more advanced techniques, a higher standard of products and greater continuity of supply.
May I quote one more paragraph, to show that somebody else thinks the problem is not purely a maritime one, but one for cooperation by Canadians everywhere:
Because of geographical disadvantages to trade with the rest of Canada, maritimers must look to the sea and to the fifteen million potential customers to the south. But they must gain access to these markets on more favourable terms than in the past if the economy is really
to develop. And this depends on national and international trade policies over which they can have no effective control. Hence the maritimers naturally hope that Ottawa will give them the appropriate tariff framework within which their export economy can properly breathe.
It is recognized that the problem is a difficult one, and I do not pretend to know all the answers, 'but I do not wish the impression to go unchallenged that we are in the predicament in which we find ourselves simply because of lack of initiative and vision. We know the difficulties and fully appreciate them. We know that we are at a disadvantage in selling to central Canadian and western markets, but on the other hand, I would emphasize that we are just as fully aware that we are favourably situated to place goods on foreign market's, by virtue of our position on the Atlantic seaboard. We have the vision to know that what we need, and want, is freer access to these markets through the medium of favourable trade agreements and tariff structures.
This is an old story, and I won't labour it further at this time. I would say, however, that we have recently made available to ravaged foreign countries vast sums in the form of loans, to make it possible for these unfortunate countries to purchase goods produced in Canada. We in the maritime provinces are more favourably situated than anybody else to deal with these foreign markets. This is one instance in which this government can apply not only vision but a fair measure of justice on its own part, and recognize that while we are at a normal disadvantage in manufacturing for the Canadian market, we have a decided natural advantage with respect to foreign markets. Those concerned with making goods available for foreign consumption through the medium of these loans should ensure that orders are placed accordingly.
In conclusion I would say that the majority of maritimers interpreted the minister's statements in the helpful spirit in which they were given. It is hoped these few remarks will help to clear up the wrong impression that has developed in the minds of some of our citizens.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject before us is recognized as one of great importance, and the debate upon it has been extremely interesting, but it does seem to me that it has wandered far afield and that it has been longer than necessary in view of the clear-cut proposal which is before us. Having said that in my view the debate has gone longer than necessary, it behooves me to state my view on the matter very briefly, and I shall do so.
Redistribution

The proposition before us has just two points, and they are direct and specific. The first relates to the method of representation of the Canadian people in this parliament. The second relates to the question as to how we should go about making any changes if it is necessary to do so to achieve the best method of representation.
With reference to the first question, we all seem agreed that representation in a democratic parliament such as ours should be by population. It has been argued in a good many speeches during the course of this debate that in the past we have not had exactly proportionate representation at any time, nor have we such representation at the present time. That is quite true, bearing in mind the points which have been made. But the fact is that the resolution before us comes closer to representation by population than anything that has yet been proposed in this parliament or to the Canadian people. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me the answer is simple-that we in this parliament ought to vote for the resolution.
I confess that I have found it difficult to follow all the arguments which have been made by speakers who professed their loyalty to this principle and yet have suggested other ways and other figures which should be arrived at than those which would follow from the application of this principle. But there it is. It is very simple. We believe in representation by population. The formula before us comes closer to that than anything yet proposed. Therefore we in this group are in support of the resolution.
I join with those who have expressed the view that, after the resolution has been carried and the British North America Act amended accordingly, we should pay attention more closely to that principle of representation by population. I agree that there are other considerations to be thought about, such as small provinces like Prince Edward Island and areas like the northwest territories. I agree also that there is something to be said for a smaller population per constituency in large areas such as in some of the rural parts of our country. But I suggest on the other hand that that idea has been carried too far. In a province such as my own, for example, where we have constituencies varying in population all the way from 22,000 up to 70,000. That wide discrepancy obtains not only as between rural and urban constituencies but amongst rural constituencies themselves. For example, there is one rural constituency in Manitoba with a population now of 22,000; there is another with a population of 55,000. However, the resolution

before us does not prevent adjustment of that kind of situation, and therefore, even from the position I am taking, one can have no quarrel with it. And so on the score of representation by population we in this group are in favour of the resolution.
The other question before us involved in this proposition is the method of making a change if we are agreed that change is necessary, and under that heading we have a mass of legal arguments and involved consideration of the question whether confederation is a compact, or whether Canada is a nation. I suggest that we should realize not only the force of the argument put forward the other day by my colleague the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), that what was achieved in 1867 was a nation, but also that the people of Canada to-day think of this country not as a collection of sovereign states but as a nation; and on that basis we should act in this matter.
I agree with those who contend that the amendment of our constitution should be in Canadian hands, and also that the formula for amending it should be definitely worked out and laid down. But pending that, I do not think we should act in any way that would make us less than a nation. We should not return to the status which this land held when it was a collection of individual colonies. Rather we should regard this matter as one that is of concern to all the people of Canada as Canadians, and one that should be decided in the place where the people are represented as Canadians.
The Minister of Justice made one statement which has elicited replies from various members which, I suggest, has taken the discussion a little wide of the mark. I refer to his suggestion that the provinces are represented here by the members from the various provinces. In reply to that, hon. members have made the statement that they do not feel that they represent their provinces, and so the argument has gone back and forth on that point. What we should realize is that in this house we do not represent provinces. We do not, if we appreciate our position correctly, represent our people on a provincial basis. We represent Canadians. I do not presume to represent the province of Manitoba. I represent 60,000 Canadians who happen to live within the province of Manitoba, and my concern is to represent them with respect to their Canadian interests. Their Canadian interests are decided here in this parliament, and we should think of the matter on that basis. On the score of method as well as on the score of basis of

Redistribution
representation, the resolution hits the mark and therefore the vote of this house should be in favour of it.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Is the hon. member not aware that when I spoke of the provinces being represented here I particularized my remarks very carefully? I stated, as appears at page 1936 of Hansard:
Another question, which has arisen each time there has been any move to ask for an amendment of the British North America Act, has been whether or not the provinces had been consulted and had agreed to it. I think that when the question is put in that form it is ambiguous. The provinces, that is to say the people of the provinces, are all represented in this parliament, and for the purposes of such matters as are confided to the jurisdiction of this parliament it is by those representatives here that the people of the provinces speak.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I am glad that the Minister of Justice has interjected into the record that quotation from his speech. I recognize that in that statement he made the point I am trying to make. But my contention is that the position he took has been misunderstood and it has been thought of by some members in the house in the terms I suggested earlier.
One other comment I wish to make is this. It is deplorable that sectionalism should have crept into the debate to the extent that it has. Sectionalism has been with us not only in the speches of some members from the different provinces who have tried to state the ease for more members for their particular provinces; it is also involved in the whole argumenj, that the matter should be referred to the several provinces. My objection to sectionalism and my desire for everything possible in the direction of Canadian unity is not just for the purpose of intellectual tidiness, but rather because I feel that nothing can more successfully retard social and economic progress in this country than the attempt to keep us divided. We have had examples of this in connection with the dominion-provincial conference, which has been referred to so often in this debate. For several months now the Canadian people have been hoping that, in consequence of the proposals made to that conference, a better old age pension scheme and a health insurance plan were just around the corner. Maybe they are still around the corner, but it becomes a very long comer because of provincial superintendence, if I may use the phrase of the Minister of Justice, over national affairs. The whole question of social security, labour legislation and other matters in these fields are of concern to all citizens of this land. These things are our concern as Canadians, right across the country, and to the extent that the forces of
reaction can keep us arguing over provincial rights, and can keep us divided on provincial, racial or any other lines we delay the possibility of dealing with these important social and economic problems. I hope that in future debates in this house we shall give serious thought to what sectionalism does to the expectations of the Canadian people for a better life, for better social and economic conditions. To keep sectionalism alive is surely, in this day and age, unthinkable. We all feel that the united nations organization will succeed only if we surrender a measure of our national sovereignty and become one world, and surely we should no longer have to argue the point that within this country we are not nine separate sovereign states, but one Canada, the main concern of which should be the best possible life for all Canadians.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Inasmuch as I have been interested for some time in one phase of the discussion on this question there are a few thoughts to which I should like to give expression, and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, and the house, that I shall endeavour in doing so to be as brief as I possibly can, and to the point. As I have said on previous occasions, in discussing this matter I have never presumed to pose as a constitutional or legal expert. On each occasion on which I have spoken on this question I have said that I considered the issues which were involved were those with which every individual citizen of Canada should be familiar; and it is only the fundamental and basic principles that I wish to concern myself with in this discussion to-day.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) raised the essential principle which is involved in this discussion. He pointed out that in the government's endeavour to eliminate an injustice with respect to the distribution of dominion seats, a fundamental principle was involved, namely, a method of amending the British North America Act. I believe that that principle raises the whole fundamental question of how we are to proceed with amendments to the British North America Act in the future. Certainly this is not going to be the last occasion on which discussions are to arise as to ways and means of amending the British North America Act.
One question that comes to my mind-it has been raised by many hon. members who have already spoken-is this: Why does the British North America Act not contain a definite procedure which can be followed in amending the act? Why has the British North America Act no provision of that kind? Speaking on this point, the Minister of Fisheries
R p. distribution

(Mr. Bridges) suggested that it was a mere oversight on the part of the fathers of confederation. From what little reading I have done on the subject I personally cannot credit them with being guilty of an oversight upon such a fundamental question. The hon. member for Eglinton went further and suggested that it was because the fathers of confederation could not agree. He did not support his contention with any evidence, which I should like to have seen him do. From my study and reading I feel that the reason there is no provision in the British North America Act for its amendment is far more fundamental than the reasons advanced by these two hon. gentlemen.
I would suggest that the whole constitutional position of this country is on an unsound basis, and that accounts for the fact that there is no provision in the act for its amendment. There are many things with which we are dealing in these days which indicate that. On every occasion that an amendment must be made, a debate arises of the kind that we have been having for the past few weeks. We have the question of the flag, appeals to the privy council, the matter of the disallowance of dominion and provincial legislation, the matter of an appointed upper house, and so on. These are all anomalies in our constitutional position. They, and the lack of any recognized way of amending the British North America Act, are symptomatic of the fact that there is something fundamentally not right in our whole constitutional basis.
We proclaim that we are a nation, that we are sovereign, that we are politically independent of the imperial parliament. We have been proclaiming that ever since the passage of the statute of Westminster in 1931, and yet all these anomalies prevail to-day. Why are we confronted with this situation? Why is it that we are discussing the matter of adopting a distinctive national flag? Why were not these things taken care of in 1931? Why were not all these anomalies eliminated then. That is a pertinent point. It indicates that there is something fundamentally unsound in our whole constitutional set-up; otherwise we should not be confronted with these situations from time to time.
If we are to endeavour to lay down definite procedure for the amendment of the British North America Act in the future, whatever we do will have to be determined by what took place in 1867. Whatever we do to attempt to rectify the situation must be done in the light of what took place in 1867 at the passage of the British North America Act.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) made some points with which I should like to
[Mr. Kulll.l
deal. He made the statement that at the time of confederation the provinces were not recognized as autonomous units. His exact words were, as reported at page 2617 of Hansard:
These were colonies exercising delegated powers under the full control of the imperial parliament or the crown advised by its ministers. There is no doubt that the members of those provincial colonial governments rose above the stature of the institutions which could no longer contain them, and they succeeded in founding a Canadian nation. But they had no power to do so by contract or treaty or agreement of their own.
Does it not logically follow from that that Canada did not become a federal union in 1867? Certainly in the consummation of a federal union and a federal arrangement, federation presupposes a condition of sovereignty, and if the condition of sovereignty must precede confederation or federation, then how does that harmonize with the position which the minister claimed prevailed prior to 1867? So I think I am arguing logically when I suggest that if the provinces were not free and independent, as the minister says they were; if they were dependencies in 1867, then that which was consummated was not a federal union but rather a united colony. I think that is completely in harmony with opinions which can be brought to bear; it is completely in harmony with the preamble of the act itself, and is also in harmony with the Interpretation Act of 1889, which says that the expression "colony" shall mean-
. . . any of Her Majesty's dominions, exclusive of the British islands and of British India; and where parts of such dominions are under both a central legislature and local legislatures, all parts under the central legislature shall for the purpose of this definition be deemed to be one colony.
So if the minister's statement is correct and in accordance with the true position at that time, the condition that has prevailed ever since has been that the united colonies have been dependencies. Since that must have been so, the question I should like to ask is in what manner and by what process has Canada become a federal union and this parliament a federal parliament. A federal union and a federal parliament could be consummated only through an agreement reached by the provinces as sovereign entities. Therefore the whole constitutional position is left in a confused state, so far as I am able to understand it. On the one hand we have an act by which we are governing ourselves, which is actually an imperial statute and not a constitution proper. On the other hand we contend that we are a nation independent of the imperial parliament; yet there is nothing in the records to indicate the manner in which a federal system has arisen.

Redistribution
The only conclusion I can draw from this situation, therefore, is that when the authority which the imperial parliament exercised over the people of Canada was surrendered in 1931 through the statute of Westminster, it was surrendered to the provinces of Canada; for it is contrary to natural law that the imperial parliament could create any federal government in Canada. A federal government can be created only by the provinces which compose the union. Consequently I feel justified in asserting that the authority previously held by the imperial parliament over the colony of Canada has now been relinquished to the provinces of Canada, and remains there until such time as they create a federal union and a federal government of their own choice. If there were an agreement or compact among the provinces of Canada, surely a certified copy of it should be in the records, with rhe signatures of the appropriate authorities; but there is none. Hence the confused situation that exists in this country. We are deemed to govern ourselves by an imperial statute, while at the same time claiming that we are a nation, independent, free and sovereign. If we are a nation proper, then surely it follows that we should have the right and there should be a specific process to amend our constitution, but that is not so. We still proceed as we are doing under this measure, to the imperial parliament, petitioning them to grant us a particular amendment.
So far as rectifying this whole situation is concerned, I do not agree that it should be undertaken by this parliament, by a combination of this parliament and the provincial premiers, or by any small representative body. I believe the issues involved in removing the anomalies which exist in our whole constitutional position, including the matter of amending our own constitution, are of such fundamental importance that the people of Canada as a whole must be consulted. As far as my reading and information go the people of Canada have never been consulted on the British North America Act as a constitution. If the British North America Act is regarded as an imperial statute, they could not have been consulted in 1867; it could not be expected that they would be consulted. If it is an imperial statute, and we are to function under a proper constitution, then surely logic dictates that such constitution should be submitted to the people of Canada for ratification; and until such time as that has been done, how can it be asserted that the people are responsible for the circumstances which prevail?
I suggest that the only democratic way to take care of methods of amending the constitution in future is by consulting all the
people of Canada. The people of Australia certainly were consulted on their constitution. They were permitted to vote by ballot; in fact they voted on their constitution twice, and it did not become legal and binding until such time as a majority voted in favour of it. We in Canada claim that the British North America Act is our constitution, yet we have never been consulted on it. I have found no record to indicate that the people of Canada were ever consulted. Therefore how can it be said that there is in Canada a constitutional arrangement agreed to by the people of Canada? I suggest, therefore, that we shall never proceed in a businesslike manner, we shall always have debates and arguments and differences of opinion on this subject of amending the British North America Act, until we as a nation lay down some formula and some technique which we can follow logically from begining to end.
On previous occasions when discussing this subject I quoted at length some of those who gave evidence before the special committee on the British North America Act in 1935. Some good advice was given before that committee, and I cannot understand why parliament, having set up the committee, having summoned those who were recognized as constitutional authorities, having had those persons suggest ways and means of taking care of this situation, has never acted. Here we are to-day still debating how we are to proceed. As I say, we have had already the benefit of the deliberations of that parliamentary committee before which outstanding constitutional authorities gave their opinions and made their recommendations, and still we are carrying on in this fashion.
As I have said on previous occasions, the most democratic and best advice given on that occasion was given by Doctor Beau-chesne, the worthy Clerk of this house. I cannot understand why the government, this parliament and the provincial legislatures have not acted on that advice. I dislike repetition in myself just as much as I dislike it in anyone else, but as .this is such a fundamental matter I feel I must place on record once more the suggestions made by Doctor Beau-chesne with respect to removing the anomaly with which we are now concerning ourselves, as well as other anomalies which exist in our constitutional position. I should like to quote from page 126 of the proceedings of the special committee on the British North America Act which sat in 1935, where Doctor Beauchesne is reported as follows:
-the Statute of Westminster has altered our status . . .
Redistribution

The time has come in my humble opinion, when the British North America Act, except as to minority rights, should be transformed and a new constitution more in conformity with present conditions should be adopted. Amendments here and there would be mere patchwork which could not last. The people of 1935 are different from those of 1867. What we want is a new constitution . . .
The new constitution must leave nobody with a grievance. A spirit of conciliation should predominate. For these reasons, the task must be entrusted to an independent body in which all the elements of the country will be represented. I therefore beg to suggest an imposing constituent assembly formed of eminent men coming from all parts of Canada. Provincial conferences, attended by a few ministers meeting behind closed doors, would hardly satisfy public opinion. The debate should be public . . .
I should like to interpolate there and say that I think that is the most commendable suggestion as to how to deal with this anomalous situation. It is in entire conformity wTith democratic principles, and is certainly worthy of the support of the people of Canada. As Doctor Beauchesne indicates, the circumstances are of such a nature that this matter should not be considered by a small body of representatives of the provinces and the dominion; it should be considered by a constituent assembly elected by all the people of Canada and charged specifically to deal with this whole problem. Doctor Beauchesne went on to say:
I want the assembly to sit in a city in the west. It would not be necessary for a delegate to be a member of parliament or of a provincial legislature . . .
Then again on page 128 Doctor Beauchesne is reported as follows:
I would suggest that the assembly do not sit in Ottawa, in order that it may not have the appearance of being dominated, or even influenced by the dominion power; and, as the western provinces are of such paramount importance in the country, I suggest the best city for the representatives to gather in would be Winnipeg.
And again on page 131:
There have been many disputes about provincial rights since 1867, and it seems certain that when a new constitution is drawn up, the distribution of federal and provincial powers will have to be modified.
And again on page 135:
I think the time is ripe for a change in the constitution. I do not think you would need much publicity in order to draw to the attention of the people of this country that the British North America Act is inadequate.
And again on page 129:
Whether our country should be changed from a dominion to a kingdom is also a subject which might be discussed. I would suggest that the country should be called "the federated states of Canada."
[Mr. Kuhl.l
I consider that a comprehensive and allinclusive suggestion as to how to rectify the present anomalies and confusing constitutional position. I cannot understand why the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and the representatives of the provinces have not considered carrying out that proposal. This parliament appointed a special committee to study this subject, and here are the recommendations that were made. Surely there could not be a more democratic way to deal with it; consequently I again suggest and urge and recommend that at the earliest opportunity the suggestions of Doctor Beauchesne be implemented.
There could not be a more logical place in which to do that than the dominion-provincial conference. On the last occasion on which I spoke on this subject I said that I would be watching carefully to see what the delegates might have to say on this particular subject, but I must confess that I have been disappointed. I still hope that we may see the day when someone will take up Doctor Beauchesne's proposals and initiate action along that line. I believe it is only by adopting such a procedure that we can democratically and in the interests of all sections of Canada rectify the present unsatisfactory constitutional position.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although this question has been under consideration for a number of sitting days, because of its importance I feel not at all disposed to apologize for expressing my views upon it. It has been said during this debate that the question under discussion is one of the most important that we have had to deal with over a very long period of time. I perfectly agree with that view. We are not to-day proposing to amend the Confederation Act of 1867 in the same manner and for the same purposes as we have done in the past. We are dealing to-day with the very foundation of the representation of the provinces in the dominion parliament. We are in a way affecting the basis or foundation of the pact of confederation which has been for a number of years now the source of our liberties and the source of all our powers, politically speaking, socially speaking, and nationally speaking. Therefore we should not approach such a problem without very serious consideration of the consequences of our action.
Being of this view, I regret that such a question has not been, from the very beginning, declared by the government and by the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) a free question upon which all members of the House of Commons would be at

Redistribution
liberty to express their own personal views and the views of the province which they represent in this house, without fear of being jeopardized in their relations with the party at present in power. This question is so important that it should be dealt with from a general, yes, from a national point of view, and not from the narrow point of view of a majority in this house or of a political party in power. It is too important a question to be left to the authority of the government in power or to a majority in this house.
As I said, by this resolution we are touching the very basis of our political, social, and national life, and nobody can say how far we are going to go along that line and what will be the consequences of our action.
It is unfortunate also, Mr. Speaker, that in relation to such an important problem as the amending of our constitution we should proceed in the same manner as if it were proposed that the house should sit on Wednesday night-by a simple resolution presented by a minister, and upon which there can be only one kind of debate, what we generally call a full-dress debate, when no questions can be asked of the minister introducing the resolution, and when no elucidation of any difficult point can be made. We are bound, when this resolution is submitted to a vote, to say yes or no without having had the opportunity of inquiring about the details of the motion and receiving definite answers from the minister, and without having had the advantage and benefit of the views of persons knowing something about constitutional law who are unable to express their views in the House of Commons because they are not members. It is unfortunate, I repeat, that an amendment to our constitution is to be made in such a manner.
It is unfortunate also that we have had propounded in this house from as high an authority as the distinguished Minister of Justice that we can do this without any regard to the views of the provinces whatever may be their interest in the matter. I know there are precedents. I have been a party man and a member of this house long enough to know the precedents that have been cited during this debate. But I contend that precedents such as those that have been referred to should not be the guiding rule when we are dealing with the very basis of the representation of the Canadian people in the House of Commons.
What we are doing now is not a repetition of the precedents that have been referred to. In those days there was no question of changing the basis of representation in the House of Commons. Exceptions were made to the
general rule in favour of minorities. And when I speak of minorities I include small provinces in the Dominion of Canada, because, after all, they are minorities. Exceptions have been made to the general rule established in the constitution of 1867, and all the precedents mentioned provided for such exceptions being made to remedy a difficult situation existing with respect to the smaller provinces. But here we are changing the very basis of the . representation in the house, and we discard the principles and ideas exposed when the act of 1867 was put into force and effect and as they have been interpreted since, on many occasions.
To say that Ottawa is the only authority to amend our constitution, even concerning matters in which the provinces may be interested, is in my humble judgment going a little bit too far. It was never in the mind of the fathers of confederation that the federal parliament would have authority, without the consent of the provinces, without even the courtesy of consulting them, to change dispositions of the act which are material to their welfare and which are essential to the preservation of their way of life, their traditions, laws and liberties.. It was never in the minds of the fathers of confederation that parliament would be vested with such wide authority.
And what is the consequence? We have heard the Minister of Justice say in reply to the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr Smith) that the federal parliament would have the authority to make representations to the imperial parliament to amend the constitution by wiping out section 133 of the British North America Act which protects the French language in this country, and that without consulting the provinces. That is one consequence of the theory which has been expounded by the Minister of Justice in this house, contrary to the views expressed by his distinguished predecessor, the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, and all public men in Canada since 1867.
In all the discussions which took place in regard to amending the constitution' it has always been contended by all parties that we could never touch the privileges of any province, of any race or any religion, without giving them the opportunity of being consulted and of expressing in detail their views on the proposition.
The Minister of Justice rested his case, if I understood him aright, on Professor Kennedy's work on constitutional law. Not later than an hour ago I happened to open the report of a committee which sat in 1935 to consider the constitution of Canada and the proposals
Redistribution

for amendment and the extent of the respective jurisdictions under the act -of 1867. What did Professor Kennedy contend? The minister made the argument that the federal parliament had alone the right to deal with redistribution because it was within the powers attributed to the house, but that we would have no right at all to deal with the rights reserved to the provinces by sec. tion 92. When Professor Kennedy appeared before the committee in 1935 he said clearly, in answer to questions put to him, that the federal parliament could make representations to the imperial parliament to amend the constitution even on matters covered by section 92, and defining the privileges and the authority of the provinces. So, if the federal case rests on the views of Professor Kennedy, we must conclude, from the proposal now oefore the house, that the federal authority claims in fact the right to invade provincial rights and to deprive the provinces of the jurisdiction and powers which were given to them by section 92 of the British North America Act.
If Ottawa enjoyed jurisdiction in matters of that kind, it would amount to the very thing which many Canadians were afraid of at the time of the passing of the act-legislative union. That interpretation would give the House of Commons the authority to deal with everything, including matters of education as well as matters of language and religion. I object to such an interpretation, and I do not want to see the federal authority have the power to deprive the provinces of even the least of the privileges which were given to them.
"Balkanize Canada"! This is a wrong expression which is being popularized because it is a nice-sounding term. Canada is what she is to-day because of the strength of the different provinces, because Canada is a confederation and not a country governed solely by the authority which legislates in Ottawa.
Let us see, Mr. Speaker, how the new theory is applied in the field of practical politics. The contention is that there is no necessity to consult the provinces, that the provinces have no right to dictate to the government in such a matter, that they have no authority to express their views on such a question. I say that it was not the case in 1943. In that year the federal parliament listened to the voice of two provinces, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and the resolution which was then presented to the house, to postpone redistribution until after the war, was passed at the request and ait the insistence of those two provinces. It is to the credit of the min-

isters who represented Saskatchewan and Manitoba in the cabinet that such a thing was done. The government then showed that they were ready to listen to the voice of two provinces, and the ministers from these provinces indicated that they were not only representing Canada as a whole but were thinking first of their own provinces. They insisted upon obtaining the postponement of redistribution in 1943 against the will of the province of Quebec. Sometimes I envy the courage and solidarity of the representatives of the other provinces, and I wish that we in the province of Quebec had the same amount of solidarity and courage to claim what is our due and to insist on our privileges and our liberties.
"Balkanize Canada"! Is the British commonwealth of nations a Balkanized organization? The British commonwealth of nations is composed of nations who claim independence for themselves. The provinces can exert a certain amount of independence. at least in the field which is allotted to them, and to do so is not to Balkanize Canada in any way, shape or form. The opposite would be centralization. And what has centralization done to the world0 It gave Mussolini to Italy; it gave Hitler to Germany. That is the result of centralization. In the centralized organization the value of the individual disappears; he is absorbed in the great mass of the majority, and his identity and personality are lost.
It has been contended that we who come from the different provinces represent the provinces. I claim that we do not represent the provinces. We represent constituencies in the Dominion of Canada, but we do not speak for the provinces as such. We have not the authority to speak for the provinces. We can speak as members for the constituencies which have done us the honour of electing us to this house, but we are not representing the provinces. We are members of the federal parliament coming from different sections of the country, but, I repeat, we cannot speak for the provinces. It would be a little boastful on our part to say that we alone can speak for the provinces, that we alone have the proper light on the general problems affecting the provinces and the country as a whole. That is a mistaken view.
I submit that the constitution of 1867 is a document-call it a statute if you will; call it a pact or a compact-it is a document that must be taken in its entirety and cannot be torn apart so that we can say that on a particular section of the law of 1867 we are masters and can do what it pleases us to do, while on other sections of the pact of

Redistribution
1867, the provinces have the authority. That is a mistaken attitude. We have to accept the pact of 1867, or the statute of 1867, as a whole or discard it. It has been established after many conferences, and it is the result of a compromise, even if it is now in the form of a statute.
I know it has been argued by the very pleasant Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bridges), and by the distinguished Minister of Justice that we could deal with certain sections which are more clearly within our jurisdiction, and not touch others. May I repeat here that the doctrine upon which the Minister of Justice rested his case is the doctrine of Mr. Kennedy, who says that we can even interfere with the powers that have been given the provinces.
That opinion or view, that the act of 1867 is a statute which can be amended by the imperial parliament on the recommendation of the federal parliament, in certain cases-to accept the views of some members who have spoken-without the consent of the provinces, is a view that is new. In the past it has always been contended that at least in matters of importance the provinces should be consulted particularly on questions in which they thought they Bad an interest. Even on the question of redistribution the provinces are interested. They are as much interested as the federal parliament.
It is true that the parliament at Ottawa has the authority to divide the country into a certain number of seats, to fix the limits of those seats; but the number of representatives in any province in Canada is something that concerns and interests all the provinces. The provinces have the right to be consulted when we change the number of their representatives or when we adopt measures which are capable of modifying their representation in this House of Commons.
This has been the interpretation of all parties. It has been indicated, though not too clearly or too definitely, that certain elements in certain provinces were interested in creating difficulties for the federal authority. Reference has been made to the present government of Quebec and the present government of Ontario. Let me say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the representatives of all sections of Canada, that what has been said by these provincial premiers reflects the opinion of all the members of their respective legislatures. What has been said by the present premier of the province of Quebec has been said by the Liberals of the province of Quebec sitting in the provincial house.
The protest I am making now is the same protest I made in 1943. That protest I made
in 1943 has been supported by as good a Liberal as the hon. Mr. Godbout, who was premier of Quebec, on June 22, 1943, when he wrote to the Prime Minister of Canada, as follows:
Dear Mr. King:
I regret to hear that you consider delaying the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons according to the 1941 census. This decennial readjustment is an essential part of the compact between the provinces out of which arose the Canadian confederation, and therefore the British North America Act cannot properly be amended, in this respect, without the assent of the provinces.
This is not the Hon. Mr. Duplessis or the Hon. Mr. Drew; it is the present leader of the Liberal forces in the province of Quebec, and the man who is followed by most of the members from the province of Quebec sitting in this house. He concludes this letter:
I have no doubt that due consideration will be given to these representations, and I sincerely hope that no attempt will be made to have the British North America Act amended against the wishes of this province.
These are the words of the then premier of Quebec, the Hon. Mr. Godbout, in 1943; and what is being said by others to-day is only a repetition of what Mr. Godbout himself said in Quebec.
Later, in 1944, there was a debate on this question in the provincial legislature of Quebec and one of the brightest members of the Godbout government, Hon. Hector Perrier, a man of knowledge and experience, a talented man, said, according to the report:
(Translation):
Speaking on behalf of the government, the Hon. Hector Perrier emphasized the strong stand taken by the Prime Minister last year. He added that if the federal elections take place under a redistribution scheme contrary to the constitution, it will be our duty to protest.
(Text):
May I translate the quotation. Mr. Perrier agreed with the energetic attitude taken by the then premier of the province, Hon. Mr. Godbout, in the previous year. He added that if federal elections took place in accordance with a redistribution which is not in conformity with the constitution our duty will be to protest. That is the attitude and the language of a man of authority. It was the attitude of the Liberal party in Quebec, to which I have given the best years of my life and the strength of my health.
I am in favour of unity, but I am against unification. I am in favour of unity and union of all the contracting parties to the pact of confederation, but I want to respect the privileges, rights and liberties of all the component parts of the Dominion of Canada. This question is so important that it should
Redistribution

have been submitted to a conference of some kind, or at least to a committee, before which
all interested parties would have had the privilege of appearing and expressing their views.
It has been said that in framing the constitution of 1867 representation by population was contemplated. Yes, that was the object and the intent of the fathers of confederation. Have we that measure? We have not representation by population, having made many exceptions to the rule. At the present time we are going even a step farther. The representation of Prince Edward Island is to remain as it is. I am in favour of that, but in so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned it is not representation by population. So far as New Brunswick is concerned it is not representation by population. So far as Nova Scotia is concerned it is not representation by population. I say that the proposed amendment goes a step farther. The exceptions are not being disturbed by the present resolution, not at all. The step farther that we are taking is that we state here that if one of the provinces suffers a reduction in its population to such an extent that the number of representatives might be fewer than the number of senators, then the number of representatives in the House of Commons should be fixed at the number of representatives in the Senate, and that in any future calculation for the representation in the House of Commons the population of that or those provinces will not be taken into account. That is section 4 of the bill which it is proposed to send to the imperial parliament to amend our constitution. Therefore, if any of the maritime provinces or any other has a reduction in population and is exposed to a decrease in the number of representatives to a number fewer than the representatives in the senate, the population of those provinces will not be counted when ascertaining what population will justify electing a member to the House of Commons. We are told that this will be representation by population. It is not representation by population at all.
Some other people try to justify their attitude by saying that it is to correct an injustice. Such injustice could have been corrected otherwise. The injustice which Quebec suffered could have been corrected in 1943. Quebec agreed to the fixing of members for Prince Edward Island and the maritime provinces, but I do not want the same exception to the rule being applied to other provinces in Canada. But we are not correcting the injustice. We had only to listen to the speech delivered by the brilliant Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to learn 
that. He easily dispelled the illusion of some hon. members that this resolution had been prepared to correct an injustice. He said that was not the purpose of the resolution. Therefore he did not agree with those who try to find comfort in the proposed increase of the number of representatives from Quebec.
Yes, Quebec is being given eight more members, but we have to agree to Saskatchewan receiving three or four more than she is entitled to; to Manitoba having three more according to the B.N.A. Act as it stands. We have also to agree to Ontario having one more than she is at present electing, and to British Columbia having two more. We are to have eight additional members, but the rest of Canada are to have eleven more members. That is the consolation that is being offered and the illusion that is being created in order to get our friends to agree, and this without consulting the provinces. Parliament is presently doing what the Hon. Mr. Godbout and others opposed in 1943. We are agreeing to something which is the very opposite to what he proposed-consultation with the provinces.
I do not wish to proceed any longer. In closing, I wish to impress you, Mr. Speaker, and my colleagues in the House of Commons, with the fact that in expressing my views I have been unable to be different from what I have always been.
I have been unable to avoid arguing my point without a certain amount of heat. It is my nature, my temperament; and to those of my party I can only say, as a justification or excuse, that they did not complain of my temperament in the past. They had no objection in the past when I was arguing my case in the same way as I am now presenting it to the House of Commons. My campaigns in the province of Quebec on behalf of my 'party for the last thirty-five years were carried on in the same tone, with the same voice and the same element of sincerity I am exemplifying to-day. I am ageing, but I am the same man I have always been; and even if my views are not in accord with the views of those to whom I have the honour of addressing myself at the present time, I ask that they be treated as the opinion of a sincere man who tries to express himself in his own personal way; who presents his arguments as best he can in the interest of his constituents and in the interest of his fellow Canadians.
Whatever was the tone of my remarks; whatever terms I have used; whatever way I have expressed views, I have always been a Canadian to the core. Though I am attached to the privileges, rights and liberties promised

Redistribution
to my province, I do not want to be looked upon as a narrow-minded Canadian, but rather as a Canadian capable of looking upon his country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I am not an isolationist. I am a Canadian, strongly in favour of preserving the liberties, rights and privileges of all the component parts of Canada, and I want them to be respected on all occasions and in all circumstances.
I had something else to say. I imagine I am near the limit of my time and I do not want to transgress and speak any longer than I should. I want to close, Mr. Speaker, by saying that I am going to vote in favour of the amendment, because it supports the principle of consultation with the provinces. I am not scrutinizing the motives or interest that may be in the minds of some people who have been supporting the amendment, any more than I am scrutinizing the ideas and motives of other hon. members in this house. I am taking the resolution as it stands. I am taking the amendment as it is and, as it is worded. The amendment asks for consultation with the provinces and the obtaining of at least their advice before proceeding with the resolution. I am in accord with that view, and in that stand I remain in the family of the old Liberals among whom I have been brought up in my political life. I stand with Blake; I stand with Laurier; I stand with Lapointe, and on that constitutional issue I also agree with leaders of the Conservative party in the past. No, I am not alone. I am at present preaching the gospel they all have preached, the gospel I myself have been advocating in my province and in Canada as a whole for the last thirty-five years.
I was in favour of redistribution being carried out in 1943 according to the principles of the constitution of 1867, meaning that I wanted the representation in the House of Commons to be as nearly as possible according to population. I am still in favour of redistribution being carried out. If the government persists in claiming that it alone has the absolute power to deal with the question, and if the amendment suggesting consultation with the provinces is rejected, I shall then have no other alternative but to vote for the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, whatever may have been the intention of those who have moved it, the practical effect of this amendment would be to kill the main resolution. This debate clearly shows that it is imperative that some thought be given to the drawing up of a method for the discussion of constitutional matters, so that this country may be spared the judicial insecurity which now exists, and I need not emphasize that such a discussion should be held in close cooperation with the various provincial authorities. But, in view of the proposed amendment, and under the present circumstances, when the sole effect of the resolution will obviously be to do justice to the province of Quebec, I wonder why we, from that province, should have to assume all the expenses and accept all the risks of a dilatory procedure, to put it mildly, when in the past action taken without our consent and to our detriment, has so often deprived us of certian fundamental rights?
Mr. Speaker, I shall vote against the amendment, I am quite convinced that I shall thereby be rendering a loyal service to my compatriots; and taking a stand likely to bring closer together the rightminded elements of the two racial groups. Finally, I am confident that I shall thus uphold in our province and in a practical way, the democratic system. What will happen now if the amendment is defeated? We shall revert to the main resolution which, in turn, will carry or be rejected. If it be rejected, we shall nevertheless be compelled to go on with redistribution, as provided for in the British North America Act. But how shall we go about it? We shall have to choose between the various schools of thought as to the meaning of the section dealing with the ratio of twentieth. How shall we appraise the decrease in the population of a province in relation to the total population of Canada? Shall we do so in relation to the last readjustment, as referred to by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), or on the basis of the last census, as was done in the past?

I admit, Mr. Speaker, that I have been deeply impressed by the theory so ably propounded by the hon. member for Stanstead, but I cannot fail to realize that it finds opposition in many a precedent and in a judgment of the Lords of the Privy Council. Under the circumstances, I cannot take upon myself to expose my fellow citizens to a risk I myself should be unwilling to face.
Besides, in refusing to support this resolution, may I count on the adoption of a basis of representation in the House of Commons that will be fairer, more equitable, more consistent with sound democratic principles? I quite frankly confess that I cannot. My plain duty therefore is to accept it loyally, and to share both its merits and its responsibility. I feel all the freer in supporting it that it does not modify, but on the contrary, reaffirms the principle of the confederation compact. It redresses an injustice to the province of Quebec.
Finally, if, as I hope, the resolution carries, what will happen? I do not see the necessity of reading the text of a document we have been discussing for weeks. I feel I accurately sum up its meaning when I state that it confirms the principle of representation according to population. It will remedy the glaring injustice of the present system and restore the Canadian citizen's status of equality before the House of Commons.
In order to oppose the measure now under review, certain reasons have been advanced upon which I should like to dwell briefly before resuming my seat.
The first objection was raised against the surplus expenditures entailed by an increase in representation. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the danger and futility of such an argument is self-evident, when it is recalled that the very ones who are opposing to-day an average contribution of less than three cents yearly per family for the establishment of democracy at home, were voting willingly $19 billions, or an average of $7,600 per family, for the defence of democracy in the world.

When it was decided in 1943 to postpone readjustment of representation, discussions arose about the census, but it was agreed then that redistribution would be adjourned until the first session following the termination of hostilities and not until after the next census.
Finally, opponents of the resolution point out the danger to minorities arising out of the violation of provincial autonomy. This contention would carry more weight had not most [DOT] of those who uphold it now ignore 1 or fought against it in 1943, when the proposal notwithstanding the merits of the reasons which secured the approval of a majority in this house, gave rise to an injustice against which only a few Quebec members protested. There is no inconsistency, as some have suggested, in the stand taken by those who, after having opposed the 1943 resolution, support that of 1946. In 1913, an injustice would have resulted from that resolution, while in 1946 the object of the resolution is to correct an injustice the perpetuation of which would suit some people. In either case, they have fought valiantly to ensure the triumph of justice. In either case, they have endeavoured to support what they deemed just and fair.
We have been warned against abandoning the system in which Quebec is the pivotal province. But for eighty years this system has been working against common sense and against us. Certainly if the object of the resolution were to do away with provincial boundaries in regard to the representation in the House of Commons, no one would oppose it more strongly than I. But such is not the case. On the contrary, the resolution confirms the separate identity of the provinces. After the unit of representation has been determined, the population of each of the provinces is divided by that unit. Is this not an efficient and formal recognition of the separate identity of each of the provinces?
The resolution must be considered as it is, without ascribing to it consequences which it does not imply. I would like to know how the application in the House of Commons of the principle of representation based on population can infringe upon the rights of a minority.
Further, the chief practical result of the resolution will be to give to the province of Quebec the additional eight members to which

it is entitled according to its population. I would like to know which rights of which minority would be interfered with.
But I know quite well the objection raised by those who contend that it is not the immediate result of the resolution which is to be feared, but the far-off consequences of what is claimed to be a dangerous precedent. If it is a precedent, let us agree upon its nature. If it is a precedent, it is a novel one. inasmuch as it will redress an injustice.
Several amendments to the constitution were passed without previous consultation with the provinces. Such was the course adopted in 1871, a second time in 1875, a third time in 1886, a fourth time in 1915, a fifth time in 1916, and a sixth time in 1943. Shall we be so naive as to refrain from resorting to a precedent-even if one were involved, which is not the case-which would serve our legitimate interests and the cause of common sense when, invariably such precedents are applied successfully against us?
Furtl r, it has been shown that the resolution j w before the house will not bring about an amendment to the federal compact, even if we change its wording. The hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie has supported this view which is confirmed by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) and, to a large extent, by the hon. member for Stanstead.
Mr. Speaker, several authorities and statements by politicians have been quoted on the nature of our constitution; shall we be taken in, however, by academic speeches and theories, since some of the very men who wrote or spoke on the subject, flatly contradicted in practice the doctrines set forth in books or speeches?
Mr. Speaker, I loyally support this motion; however, I consider as a humiliation the fact that this house has to crawl before a foreign parliament in order to settle the problem of representation in the Canadian commons. I hope that, before the next general elections, this procedure, together with the appeals to the privy council, both of which are vestiges of a colonialism incompatible with the dignity of a sovereign state, will have disappeared from our statutes.
