Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak at this time, I do so because the remarks I am going to make could not have been made on the amendment, and the amendment which I propose to move at the end of my remarks
could not have been offered as an amendment to the amendment. It is not so much with what the resolution proposes to do that I am concerned as with one or two omissions or deficiencies in the resolution itself. I had hoped that these omissions would be explained by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) when he made his eloquent explanation of the bill, but since that was not done I feel that I should call to the attention of the house what I regard as grave omissions from the resolution as it stands at present.
This resolution purports to put the representation of the House of Commons on the basis of representation by population. I use the word "purports" advisedly, because I do not think the resolution accomplished that aim. As far as the people of the country are concerned, the most immediate effect of the resolution is to increase the membership of this house by ten at a cost to the country of $60,000 a year in indemnities alone. At a time when there is a demand from coast to coast for rigid public economy, when people are hoping that next week the Minister of Fin, ice (Mr. Ilsley) will be able to announce subs.antial reductions in taxation, I think we should give careful scrutiny to such an increase
the cost of conducting the business of the
mse of Commons, especially in view of the f, X that last fall we increased our own indem-nr.ies, rightly I believe, by fifty per cent. There was considerable criticism of that increase in some parts of the country, though I am glad to say that in my riding there was little criticism. On the contrary, both trade unions and the boards of trade endorsed the action then taken. They said that if such compensation would allow a member to represent his riding better they were for it.
That brings me to the first point I wish to make. There are many private members in this house-and I am in the class to which I refer-who are not representing their constituencies as well as they might, not because of lack of compensation, not because of lack of ability or of any desire to represent their constitutents properly, but because of the deplorable working conditions, the absence of proper office space, the absence of proper secretarial help, the total lack of any research assistance in the library, and, so far as those unfortunate members in the far corner of the house are concerned, the lack of any method by which they can properly follow the debates in this house.
I had intended to speak on this matter when the estimates of the House of Commons came up for consideration, since that is the proper time; but since the government by this resolution proposes to aggravate the situation by
Redistribution

pumping ten more M.P.'s into already crowded offices, this is the proper time, in my opinion, to bring the matter to the attention of the house and of the government. Normally I would be wasting my time telling my audience, who are mostly private members, of these disabilities; but it is a curious thing that neither the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who is leading the government, nor the Minister of Justice, who sponsors the bill, nor the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who apparently drafted it, has been a private member in this House of Commons. These hon. gentlemen have been either ministers of the crown or leaders of the opposition, and so have enjoyed good office space, adequate secretarial help, research assistance and certainly excellent seating space in the centre of the house.
Therefore I am going to indicate briefly to them some of the disabilities that private members labour under. Because of attendance in the house and committees the only time a member has for correspondence and interviews is from nine to eleven o'clock in the morning, from two to three o'clock in the afternoon and from seven to eight o'clock at night. Other hours are occupied in attending committee meetings and attending in the house as hon. members should. It is impossible to dictate, or even to try to dictate, letters when your office-mate-and most of us share offices -is 4 yard away dictating to his secretary. Under such circumstances it is also impossible to concentrate on the study of a bill or the preparation of a speech. It cannot be done while your office-mate is dictating at the same time. More than that, it is embarrassing to members. It is more embarrassing to constituents who come to see their member on matters affecting them, and are forced to discuss these matters in the presence of a third person who is a stranger. Most members, of course, withdraw to the hallway when such things take place, but there is no reason why a member of parliament should spend most of his time out in the hallways.
No business firm in this country would pay an executive $6,000 a year and then not give him a proper place in which to work. The real irony of the situation, however, is that this magnificent new parliament building has adequate office space for members of parliament. Unfortunately, because of the encroachment, throughout the years members of the staff are now using large offices which should be occupied by members of parliament. The greatest encroachment takes place between parliaments when there is no Speaker, and our genial friend, Doctor Beauchesne, is supreme. I need only remind hon. members that at the end of the last parliament there were two offices 
on the top floor which were occupied at that time by the leader of the Social Credit party in this house, but he has been moved out of those offices and the offices have been taken over by the manager of the restaurant. The point is, is it better for a member of parliament to be moved out of an office to find a place for the manager of the restaurant? There is the old story of the Arab, the camel and the tent. I do not need to tell it here, but the camel got his nose in to keep warm, and in the end the camel was in the tent and the Arab was outside. If this procedure goes on, in a few years we shall be working in the pool and the stenographers and staff will be occupying all the rooms. We need only to walk around the ground floor of this building and see the offices occupied by minor officials of the House of Commons. You need only to walk along the fourth and fifth floors of this building and see office after office occupied by secretaries of committees. These are valuable men, and they deserve office space, but the space for them is over in the west block. There should be a tunnel between these two buildings, and members of parliament should be allotted the space occupied by these men. Probably that would mean the displacement of some department in the west block, but these enormous national defence buildings which were built as headquarters for our huge wartime army must now have space which could be occupied by the displaced department, despite the objections of the permanent force empire builders.
The situation has become so bad in the offices of the press gallery that some of the gentlemen of the press are forced to work in one of the corridors in this building. Such a move as I suggest of putting the staff over in that building would give decent accommodation to the gentlemen of the press.
The second disability is secretarial help. Very few private members to-day have what a business firm would consider a good secretary. Some of them have good stenographers, but the reason there are not more good secretaries is that the girls are here for only three or four months, and there is a lack of security. They come here for a session and they have not the protection of the civil service. At the end of the session they go, and some of them are fortunate enough to get a permanent job. If they get that job they stick to it. If we had even a fraction of the secretarial help which the United States Congress provides for its congressmen and senators we would be able to do a much better job.
A third thing is the absence of research assistants in the library. Anyone who has

Redistribution
gone to a university and has done research work does not find it too great a problem to dig out and assemble material. But. as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) and the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) said yesterday, this is not a good library so far as ease of digging out the necessary documents is concerned. However, quite a few members of the House of Commons are not university graduates and have not done research work; they are farmers, seamen, engineers, loggers and so forth. They have not had that training, and there is no reason why they should spend hours of their time foraging around the library trying to assemble information which a competent research assistant would get for them in an hour. It would be very simple to acquire such people. In the universities of this country there are dozens and dozens of young men and women who are working for research degrees, their master's and their science degrees, and they would welcome the chance to come here and put in part of their time working in this library which, after all, is the best in Canada, and also meeting the members of the government and of the House of Commons and senior civil servants, the people who are running this country. They could be of inestimable value to all private members.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Han-sell) is, I believe, one of the most persistent in the matter of the great difficulty hon. members in the remote corners have of hearing speakers, especially speakers on the government benches who seem to look upon it as their chief function to relay information only to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). This problem has often been brought up in this house, and requests made for a public address system.
When we place another ten members in the far corner this chamber will be completely filled. These ten additional members will be new members and certainly will be entitled to hear all the debates in this house. I wish to make it quite clear that this is not a personal complaint on my part. I am very fortunate; as hon. members know, I share an office with one of the quietest and most industrious members here. I have one of the best secretaries in the House of Commons. It took me five years to acquire her, five years of changing a girl every session because they would go from here after the session and secure permanent jobs. However, I am forced to share her services with the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance.
As I have pointed out, university men have not the same trouble in doing research work as have members of parliament, and no member of parliament should be obliged to do work in the manner in which we attempt it, particularly when we are sent here to study policy and not be library assistants.
Lastly, thanks to the minister from British Columbia, I have a good seat in the House of Commons, but there are many members here who suffer greatly from these four disabilities.
I had hoped that the Minister of Justice would -perhaps he will when he closes the debate- indicate that the government is going to take the required action to see that the present members of parliament are given a chance to do their job in a better way by providing better working conditions.
The second omission in the minister's speech is a significant one. I have followed this long debate with the greatest of interest. I have studied science myself, and therefore I am amazed at how lawyers can start out with the same set of facts and arrive at quite different conclusions. Apparently in this resolution we are making a drastic change in our representation in this country. In other words, we are going to bring our constitution up to date to fit the needs of the country. If we are to do that, then at the same time we should change the mechanics of selecting our representatives, and bring it up to date. At the present time we elect our members by the single vote, which was good in 1867, when they had just the twro parties. It is not good now, when we have at least five national parties. How many hon. members can stand up in the house and say: "I represent the majority of the constituents of my riding?" Very few. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) is one who can do that. One member out of sixteen in British Columbia can say that, and we have five parties. The question came before parliament with the advent of the Progressive party in 1920. At that time the Prime Minister was quite inclined to try to introduce a measure of proportional representation.

That is a feeling I do not now have. I had what was considered a fairish plurality in British Columbia, but I consider that I represent only about one-third of those who cast votes in Vancouver North in the last general election. Two-thirds of the people who voted did not vote for me; and you cannot have the same confidence between a member who knows he does not represent a majority and the constituents who know the member does not represent a majority of them.
I now come to my third point, which I think represents my major opposition to the present resolution. The purpose of the resolution is said to be to bring about real representation by population. We have got rid of what the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) called one joker clause, the five per cent clause which has given Ontario an artificial membership, a greater membership than it deserves. At the same time, however, we have not got rid of the other joker clause which gives one other province, and could give other provinces, greater representation than they are entitled to on a strict representation by population basis. As far as the Yukon and the northwest territories are concerned, that can be justified because, despite the fact that they do not have the national quota, unless they are given a member for that fraction they do have they will be disfranchised. They have no provincial governments to which to turn, and few muni-

cipal governments. South of us, in the United States of America, we have the good example of a congress based entirely on representation by population, with no reservation except one, corresponding to the Yukon. When states such as Nevada and New Mexico first came into the union they did not have a population sufficient to justify a congressman, but they were given a congressman as soon as they entered the union.

speechtext:
However, when we come to the other exception, Prince Edward Island, I find it difficult to justify in my own mind, and I have not heard the Minister of Justice justify it, why this small, compact economy, which has municipal government, which has a provincial government, should be given, in fact, twice the representation given the rest of the country, by population. I agree, mind you, that Prince Edward Island is in a difficult position, but the remedy is not in creating an artificial condition in the House of Commons. The remedy is in the other chamber, where representation was set upon a regional basis. The fathers of confederation were patterning the House of Commons and the Senate, I think, quite closely on the plan followed in the country to the south.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. SINCLAIR (Vancouver North); Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was starting to comment upon what I thought was the weakness in this resolution in that it purports to be a resolution to introduce strict representation by population. I had justified, in my own mind at least, the granting of a seat to the Yukon and northwest territories, despite the fact that they have not a full quota under the present system. I had touched briefly upon the other safeguard of senate representation which is protecting Prince Edward Island at the moment. I pointed out that Prince Edward Island is a small compact economy, provided already with both municipal and provincial governments, and therefore had not the same reason to be protected as have the Yukon and the northwest territories.
I cannot understand why the government would consider objectionable the five per cent clause, that is section 51 (4), which gives to Ontario artificial representation and not at the same time remove section 51 (a) which gives to Prince Edward Island to-day, perhaps

Redistribution
to New Brunswick to-morrow, and to Nova Scotia some years hence a similar artificial representation. Such protection is not supplied to all the small provinces by that section, because in British Columbia at the moment we have six senators. That means that the only protection of this clause would come on the day when our population falls below 6/250ths of the population of Canada, or falls below 2-4 per cent of the population of Canada, which is obviously absurd.
Therefore it is apparent that this plan of representation by population rests on a very shaky foundation indeed. It rests upon this clause which introduces senate representation into House of Commons representation.
In this country in the last thirty or forty years there has been little criticism directed against the representation in this house. On the other hand, ever .since 1893 there have been continued outcries in this country against the other house; yet nothing has been done. To-day we are presented with this new system of redistribution for the House of Commons. We find that one of the pillars upon which this new redistribution bill rests is representation in our outmoded senate. As long ago as 1893 my own party was impressed with the inadequacy of the senate. I think it was at our first national Liberal convention held here in the city of Ottawa that the following plank was presented:
The present constitution of the senate is inconsistent with the federal principle in our system of government, and is in other respects defective, as it makes the senate independent of the people and uncontrolled by the public opinion of the country, and should be so amended as to bring it into harmony with the principles of popular government.
It was in 1893 also that the great Sir Oliver Mowat made an excellent speech in which he said:
The senate as now constituted is the weakest point of our constitution.
In the election of 1900, Sir Wilfrid Laurier was able to go to the country and say this about the resolutions of the 1893 convention:
This is the only plank that so far has not been effectively dealt with by the Liberal government, but the subject has not been lost sight of.
That was forty-six years ago. Just for fear hon. members may think that all the criticism of the senate has been confined to the Liberal party, I should like to read just one sentence of what R. B. Bennett said in 1915, as follows:
The senate is an irresponsible body which has thwarted the will of democracy as expressed by the House of Commons.
An interesting point about the criticism of the senate is that the strongest criticism has not come from the party in opposition but 63260-170
rather from the party which had got into power but found that it was in opposition in the senate. So that we have the Conservatives in 1915 protesting against the senate and we have the Liberals protesting at other periods against the same upper chamber. Perhaps the finest comment on our senate is found in the work of Viscount Bryce, entitled, "Modern Democracies". He spent a considerable time in discussing the upper chambers in various countries, and his conclusion is this:
Amongst these the French senate is the strongest and that of Canada, the weakest.
That again was in 1903. Therefore I feel that the greatest weakness in this resolution is the fact that it is amending the representation in this house about which there has been little criticism, when apparently nothing is being done about amending the representation in the other house, particularly when there has been so much criticism about that representation for forty or more years.
I believe in a senate or an upper chamber. I am going to quote what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said, because he expresses so well what I think about the upper chamber. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, speaking in the great debate on the senate in 1906 said, as reported at page 2301 of Hansard of April 30, 1906:
But one consideration which, to my mind, is absolutely conclusive and paramount, is that under our system of government, a second chamber is an absolutely needed safeguard for the smaller provinces against a possible invasion of their rights by the larger provinces. The system we have has been largely borrowed-not entirely, but largely-from the constitution of the American republic. As we know in that republic, the house of representatives is elected according to population. The people of the different states are represented in congress according to population. But in the American senate no such principle is admitted. In order to favour the minorities, the constitution has provided that every state, big or small, should be represented in the senate by two members.
He then went on to point out that the great state of New York had forty-five representatives and only two senators, and he referred to Vermont, which at that time had only one representative but had two members in the senate. To-day in the American congress there are four states which have only one representative each, because they have only .a fraction of the quota of population necessary to elect a representative, but every one of those states has two senators. New York has forty-five members in the house of representatives and two in the senate; Wyoming has one member in the house of representatives and two in the senate. Sir Wilfrid went on to say:
Here in our senate, as in the senate of the United States, we have not adopted the principle of representation by population. We have not

Redistribution

altogether adopted the system of the American republic, but if we were to have a reform I would not be adverse to adopting in that respect the system of our neighbours and have each province represented by an equal number of members, whether that province be large or small. This principle having been adopted admittedly for the protection of the smaller provinces, everyone will admit at once that if we were to remove that safeguard, there would be a natural discontent in the smaller provinces, so that I contend that we cannot seriously entertain, even for a moment, the idea of ever abolishing our senate. The arguments which we see from time to time in the press have altogether ignored that view of the constitution, which is a true one, and a paramount argument in favour of the maintenance of a second chamber.
I do not think the senate should be abolished as do some of my friends in the C.C.F., but I think if ever there was a time to reform the senate, it is now. The senate should be the protector of provincial rights, but it is not fulfilling that task. At this time we need as never before a strong senate which would serve as the protector of provincial rights. We have heard the speeches of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) and the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters) who emphasized the disadvantage which their province admittedly has suffered since confederation. The prairies can tell the same story.
We in British Columbia, although we are regarded as one of the rich provinces, have suffered more from domination by the two central provinces than any other part of Canada. Briefly, this is our position: We sell the things we produce, timber, fish, minerals, fruits, in the open markets of the world at low prices. We buy the things we need in the protected markets of Ontario and Quebec at very high prices. The only reason we have been able to continue, selling our products at low prices and paying high prices for what we buy, is by plundering our natural resources, robbing our fisheries, denuding our forests, high-grading our mines. That cannot go on. The same is true of the prairies.
Before the war there was a strong feeling in British Columbia for provincial rights; but, like the people of the maritimes, having seen what this country can do under strong government during the war, the people of British Columbia have resolved that we are going to go ahead as a nation and not as nine Balkan provinces. But they are reluctant to give up any authority to a central government if they are to continue to be dominated in both houses of parliament by the power of the central provinces, by high tariffs, by mountain differentials on freight rates, by trade policies that primarily help the industrial east. That is why we need a reformed senate to protect provincial rights. The fathers of con-

federation realized that. They set up a senate to represent the main divisions of Canada, Upper and Lower Canada, the maritime provinces; they gave them equal representation in the senate, twenty-four for each division, and they added a fourth division when the west was was developed and gave twenty-four to that division.
It is now time to recognize that there are five divisions. Our government does recognize that the economy of the maritimes, of Quebec and Ontario, of the prairie provinces and part of Alberta and British Columbia constitute something quite different from any other economy, but until the senate is reformed we shall continue to be dominated in the house and in the senate by the weight of numbers of the central provinces.
I am not suggesting for one moment that the senate should have five divisions of twenty-four senators. The people of Canada want a smaller, not a bigger senate. But if there were twelve members from each division, four each for Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick; twelve for Quebec; twelve for Ontario; twelve for the two prairie provinces which are so much alike, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and twelve for the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia, that is six apiece, then we should have an upper house which would prevent the colonies of Canada, because that is what the maritimes, the prairies and British Columbia have been, from being exploited by the central provinces. We would have three divisions as against two in the upper house, and the maritimes, the prairie provinces and British Columbia, would not be dominated in both houses of parliament by the central provinces.
If such a plan were adopted we would save thirty-six times $6,000-the indemnity-or $216,000, which would be quite ample to provide good secretarial help for us and the other things I mentioned a little earlier, and also provide thirty-six more offices in this building for members of parliament.
The next point is, should the senate be elected or appointed? That point was thoroughly canvassed in the great debates in this house in 1906, 1915, 1925, and it was generally agreed that because of our irregularly spaced elections for the House of Commons it would be difficult to have an elective senate. Therefore the senate may have to be an appointed body, but most people do not believe in appointment of senators for life. If the senate is to be a body that will be a check on hasty legislation obviously the term of appointment of the senators should be for more than the life of one parliament. The United States

Redistribution
provides for a six-year term. We could do the same, with one-third retiring after the end of each two years.
The most important thing about the senate from the point of view of the west and the maritimes is not whether it should be appointed or elected, but who should appoint it. That, to my mind, is the great weakness of the present situation. Two years ago, members will remember that we had a long debate on the wage control order, P.C. 9384. In setting up our national war labour board the government proposed to name equal representation for employers and for labour. Both sides objected very much, and both the national labour congresses said that if labour was to be represented they wanted to nominate their own representatives. That principle was accepted, and this principle should also apply to the senate. If the members of the senate are the protectors of provincial rights they should be appointed by the provinces, by the lieutenant-governors in council, and not by the governor general in council. The provincial governments, I am sure, would give better provincial representation. For example, in my own province we have six senators. It is a big province; yet I find from the official record that three of them reside in Victoria- one has retired-and three in Vancouver. So that there is no representation of the Fraser valley, of the Okanagan valley, of the Kootenay valleys or Cariboo and Skeena counties which are empires in themselves. Can Ontario imagine half of their senators being appointed from Toronto, the other half from Ottawa? Also, if the provincial governments appointed senators to present their problems at Ottawa, the seats in the senate would not be left vacant. In British Columbia we have had seats vacant over much too long a time.
An objection to this proposal might be that if the provinces pick the senators, the senators will have a provincial outlook. Anybody who takes part in the deliberations of the House of Commons or the Senate soon loses any provincial outlook. If Mr. Drew and Mr. Duplessis had served terms in the House of Commons or the Senate they would have been bigger and better premiers; they would have the Canadian outlook rather than the provincial outlook.
There are groups in this house that should be interested in this proposal. In Alberta, since 1935 the people have shown in no uncertain way, both provincially and federally, that they want to be represented by people who believe in the social credit philosophy. Yet in the senate, where this provincial outlook 63260-170J
should be represented, they have not a single voice. The same is true of Saskatchewan and its new party.
I had intended to move an amendment to amend sections 21 to 32 of the British North America Act to reform the Senate as well as the House of Commons. I realize how brash that would be for a young member. More properly it should be done by the government, and more properly still it should start in the senate itself. A simpler way would be to remove all mention of this outmoded senate from the present resolution. In other words, put the membership of the House of Commons on a strict representation by population basis. That would force action to be taken by providing proper senate representation to protect those areas which need protection, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, the prairie provinces and British Columbia. The effect of this would be, using the population figures of the last census, that Prince Edward Island would have two members; Nova Scotia, 13; New Brunswick, 10; Quebec, 73; Ontario, 82; Manitoba, 16; Saskatchewan, 19; Alberta, 17; British Columbia, 18. That makes 250, plus one seat for the Yukon. The 255 seats mentioned in the resolution before us is an odd figure. Obviously 250 was first tried and did not work, whatever work they had in mind for it to do. So they tried 254. A House of Commons of 250 members is a much more understandable figure for the average citizen in Canada.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) gave the impression that unless British Columbia got the twenty to twenty-one members to which we are entitled by our estimated population-according to the dominion bureau of statistics British Columbia had a population of 994.000 on December 31, 1945, as against 845.000 for Saskatchewan -we should go back to the old sixteen. I cannot agree with that. By all means we should have the two extra seats provided by the 1941 census, and if the next census gives us twenty-one members, well and good.
I hope that the Minister of Justice will comment on the four points I have mentioned. First, in increasing the membership of the house is there going to be any improvement in the conditions under which members of parliament can work? Are we to get adequate office space? Are we to get adequate secretarial help to lift the load of routine off our shoulders? Is there to be a change in the electoral system designed to suit a multiparty system such as we now have? Why is the senate not being reformed? And why is one safeguard left in this resolution which
Redistribution

makes it, not representation by population, but only slightly better than the last method of representation?
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson):
That the motion be amended:
1.	By striking out the words "two hundred and fifty-five'' in subsection 1 of the proposed section 51 of the B.N.A. Act 1867, as quoted in the resolution before the house, and substituting therefor the words "two hundred and fifty-one.
2.	By striking out the words "two hundred and fifty-four" in rules 1 and 2 of the proposed section 51 and substituting therefor the words "two hundred and fifty."
3.	By deleting rules 3 and 4 of the proposed section 51.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
have appreciated the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) who has preceded me in this debate. I share his views on the reform of the senate. 1 believe that the latter should be an elected body. Allow me, at the outset, to tender my heartiest congratulations to the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) who has delivered to-day a masterly speech. Once again he has uttered stirring words. They were the words of those who were leading the Liberal party a few years past.
When I spoke on the amendment a few days ago, I warned the government against any interference with the prerogatives of the provinces. I referred to the humiliation we felt at the thought of having humbly to petition the London government for the right to amend our constitution. I stated that this constitution is not our own, and that Canada is a country without a constitution and without a flag. However, for a number of years, without the contracting parties being consulted, with the connivance and the permission of Westminster, institutions, contracts and laws have been tampered with. The only voices which could properly be raised in protest-those of the provinces-have been silenced. An endeavour is made in this house to drown out protests under a storm of charges directed against the prime minister of Quebec. Blows are aimed at him with an ever increasing fury.
But the premier of my province rises above this useless din. He has just vindicated the jurisdiction of our legislative assemblies and upheld their cause on a plane beyond the reach of those who refuse to acknowledge a right which is theirs to exercise. He fears, as we do, a threat both immediate and remote.
Who could censure his attitude? Let us refrain from exaggeration and violence. Canada's future rests upon the cooperation of all men of good will. Even at the cost of great sacri-

flee, the Dominion government should return to the provinces the freedom to exercise their rights within the scope of their jurisdiction.
As I said before, I support this measure because I wish the influence of my province to grow in this house. I shall vote for the resolution because of its good points, provided that provincial prerogatives are respected.
Let the government cease to play with fire. Let them interfere no longer with the privileges of the provinces. Let them consult the legislatures before amending a contract which they ratified. Otherwise the government will plunge headlong into an adventure which can but lead to anarchy.
There is nothing noble or magnanimous about the attitude of the government. It reflects only a feat of strength. You will find, before long, that we are faced with new difficulties because the government neglected to consult the provinces. I object to our perpetrating an injustice for the sake of redressing a wrong. Like many others, I want to do justice to each province and trust that when the, question is put, our vote shall take into account the future and the building of a nation which can rest only on right and justice.
During the debate, I heard members emphatically declare themselves proud to take part in the amendment of the constitution. That is an illusion. We have no power to effect any change without the consent of the British House of Commons. Some members of this parliament have asserted that the British North America Act was altered several times without the provinces being consulted. They approved of such precedents. I respect their opinion but have a right to express my own. Such instances represent an abuse of power detrimental to the provinces and to minorities. If previous governments erred, why should the present authority blunder irreparably by amending the constitution without consulting the provinces?
The constitution is the guarantee of the rights of all. It is the legal consecration of the nation.
I deeply regret to find that serious-minded persons overlook the importance of protecting our rights, thinking only of the immediate advantages to be gained. It is not too late however. When the government has received from London the authority to amend the constitution, let them consult the provinces. History will emblazon the part played by the true statesmen who defend the rights of the provinces and of the minorities and will con-

Redistribution
demn those politicians who support the infringement of contracts, of the constitution and of the laws.
During the debate, the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) claimed that since 1867 French-speaking Canadians have seldom had occasion to complain of the treatment meted out to them.
I respect the minister's views, but if looking over the history of Canada I were to mention all the injustices which we have suffered, it would be an endless task. Therefore, I prefer the joint protection offered by the dominion and the provincial governments rather than entrusting solely to the central power the fate of my race, its prerogatives and its rights. Inseparable in my mind and in my heart, our constitution and the rights of minorities seem to be so closely related, that it would be heinous to entrust them to the good will of the human conscience which, alas, is so fragile and sometimes so elastic. Discussing the matter from the standpoint of plain common sense, I wish to remind the house of the seriousness of the present situation. We must keep within the bounds of moderation when dealing with such a far-reaching resolution. The nation is being led along a path which may mean the end of the Canadian constitution. Eighty years have been spent in humanizing this charter of our rights. The provinces of confederation have played their part in this work of civilization. Why not consult them?

I realize that we are presently discussing a motion dealing with the
constitution. I shall confine myself, as far as possible, to this matter and if I fail to do so,
I invite Mr. Speaker to call me to order.
On the ground of some petty political grudge of one kind or other, doubts are raised concerning the courage of the upholders of constitution. As the right hon. the Minister of Justice stated himself, is not the constitution a token of civilization? Have not those who have upheld civilization by laying down their lives; those who have fallen in the name of justice, freedom and right; those who, beyond the seas and beyond life itself, from the midst of this vast cemetery, point to the sacrifice they were worthy to make; have they not, I say, the right to demand that we honour, for the sake of Canadian unity and the future of our country, those very compacts that have been torn and trampled under foot by the dictators?
Am I in order, Mr. Speaker?
I know of a document which bears the sacred name of contract. It is the constitution of Canada. Why change this Canadian bill of rights in defiance of its drafters and without the consent of the continuators of their work? Dtfamatory charges cannot outweigh eighty years of tradition and history. If so gross an injustice is to prevail, let us seal the doom of the constitution.
But a tangible fact exists, a tangible fact remains. The British North America Act has been ratified by the provinces. Irrecusable evidence of this is found in the constitution itself. The provinces and Canada at large are even now asking us to consult them regarding this resolution. Once the British house of commons has given its consent, it will still be possible and even easy to put off changing our constitution in order to consult the provinces. It is never too late to perform an act of justice.

I should explain why I have taken the time of the house to move the amendment. There are no legal entanglements in connection with this simple alteration to the motion. May I say, sir, that I am speaking now for a number of people in Canada who are completely disfranchised, although they are just as good Canadians as any hon. member in the house. The people who live in the northwest territories have no vote and they have no representatives. They are anxious that they be granted a representative and have a voice in the government of their country. Therefore, in order that they may have that opportunity I am now speaking for them and moving this amendment, which would provide them with a representative which they desire.

I shall tell my hon. friend in a moment. I know the house is now ready for voting. This has been a long debate; I am just as ready as any other hon. member to vote on this question, and therefore I shall be as brief as possible.
Hon. members will remember that the situation was put most excellently by the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. Townley-Smith). I shall take just a few moments to summarize the main points which he made. For example, he pointed out that the total area of the northwest territories is forty-two per cent of the total land area of the Dominion of Canada and that at the present time there is only one member for that vast territory. Those who live in the northwest territories section of that half of Canada do not even have an opportunity to vote for the hon. gentleman who represents the Yukon. The Yukon area is 205,000 square miles by itself; but exclusive of the Yukon territory there rs an area of one and a quarter million square miles, with a population that is three or four times as great.
I need not point out, sir, that the natural wealth of that part of Canada is such that it might be taken for granted that in a short time there will be in that area a sufficient population to reach the unit of representation which is being provided for in the resolution. The country concerned is one of great wealth and of certain growth. I believe that that section is growing faster in population at the moment than any other part of Canada.
May I pause for a moment to point out that in a country such as ours we must take more into consideration than numbers of people

when we are dealing with redistribution? One thing that we must take into consideration, at least for some time to come, is the extent of country which it is possible for one person to represent. We have in the British North America Act a consideration also for people being represented not on a population basis. We also have a precedent in the special act which provides for a representative for the Yukon. We cannot speak now as if we were making an exception of some other section of Canada which has just as much right to representation as the Yukon or any other part of Canada which may have extra representation because of constitutional status.
The next point is that we pride ourselves on our democratic recognition of the rights of minorities. I am now speaking for a minority; it is not a racial minority. Presumably in the population of that section of the country there are peoples of all races which make up the population of Canada. It is not a religious minority. Presumably amongst that population there are people who practise all religions; but it is a minority nevertheless of all races and of all creeds. They are Canadians, and they are disfranchised.

speechtext:
The Eskimos are Canadians, if there are any Canadians, and they should have the franchise also, most decidedly. But we may come to the Eskimos some time later. I wish to confine myself now particularly to this one point. I emphasize that the people who live in the northwest territories are disfranchised. They have no say in the government of the country in which they have been born, the country in which they live, the country in which they work, and the country for which their sons fought. I think it is better that we should take time by the forelock now and meet the legitimate needs of these people before they become rebellious as people will in any part of the world who have spirit enough to rebel when they find themselves without representation, without an opportunity to take part in the government of their country, and find themselves completely neglected. That has happened in other periods o& Canadian history, and it has happened in other countries as well.
This amendment is merely the application of the democratic principle of representative government in which we pride ourselves

I have referred to the virtual disfranchisement of these inhabitants of the northwest territories. I wish to conclude, Mr. Speaker, on this note. The public business of the territory is carried on by a commissioner, a deputy commissioner and four councillors. This governing body is not appointed by the people who live there; it is appointed from Ottawa. The people have no say in who comes to Ottawa to make the appointments. The members of the governing body are mostly absentees, too, and they do not understand the conditions of the people. But the point is that the people thus governed have no say either in the selection of the apointees to whom I have referred or in the selection of the appointers of the appointees. They have no adequate and democratic way of giving expression to their grievances. They have very poor roads, and few of those, and no means of communication. Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, I had an opportunity the other day of saying something on the amendment. I advanced with as much force as I could command a proposition which seemed to me to be a reasonable one-an interpretation of section 51(4) of the British North America Act. I admit that this is not a forum in which legal arguments can achieve very much. The appraisal of arguments by majdrity is not a satisfactory way of determining their value, but I do not complain. I wish, however, that the house be made fully aware of this fact as representing the view of the party of which I am a member.
This party stands for the correction of any inequality that obtains at the present time in the representation in this house of the different provinces. May that be quite clear. The Progressive Conservative party wishes that each province be completely, fully and fairly represented in this house.
There are two questions raised by the motion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent). One has to do with fair and equitable representation and in so far as that principle is concerned this party is with him. This party regrets sincerely that for a certain period of time there should have been inadequate and unfair representation in this house of at least one province.
The other question raised is, how is this proper, fair representation to be brought about? I suggested the other day that the
very text of section 51, subsection 4, of the B.N.A. Act placed the instrument in the hands of the government and of the house. Nobody has contradicted, strange as it may seem, the interpretation that I placed upon subsection 4 of section 51. In fact, some hon. gentlemen opposite have gone out of their way to say that it is a reasonable, fair and, indeed, the only proper interpretation to be placed upon that subsection.
What is the objection? The objection is that somebody in the Department of Justice has advised that in one case this subsection has been interpreted in a way which runs counter to the interpretation that I have given. There is the issue. This judgment I have submitted has no bearing on my interpretation of section 51, subsection 4, and somebody else of experience and whose integrity I do not doubt says it has. Is the matter to rest there? It is very easy to submit this simple question to a tribunal. The machinery is available. The supreme court will even provide a special session or a special sitting to hear the issue. I know of no valid reason why the Minister of Justice himself might not go and argue the point. Whether the decision is an obiter dictum or not, does anybody think for one moment that the question which is now before the house was ever argued in all its meanings and implications before any court? To ask that question is to answer it. It was not. I submit that that is one way of dealing with this matter which is perplexing the house and possibly the government. Submit it to the courts.
There is another way of dealing with it without amending the constitution, and that way, in my submission, is found in section 52 of the British North America Act. That section states:
The number of members of the House of Commons may be from time to time increased by the parliament of Canada, provided the proportionate representation of the provinces prescribed by this act is not thereby disturbed.
I had my day in court earlier in the week and I do not wish to weary the house with a further technical legal argument. But as we have sat here we have heard praised, and rightly praised, a certain Mr. Newcombe, who was deputy minister of justice for many years and later became Mr. Justice Newcombe of the Supreme Court of Canada. He in one instance apparently gave an interpretation of section 51(4) that I do not share. But this is what Mr. Newcombe says of section 52 and the use to which it may be put. Speaking in the Prince Edward Island case, as reported in volume 33 of the Supreme Court Reports at page 645, Mr. Newcombe says:

I submit that section 52 has no office whatever so far as the present inquiry is concerned; section 52 has never yet been invoked by parliament. The power given under that section has never been executed, but it may be executed and only in one way-that is, by increasing the number fixed for the province of Quebec. If parliament were to provide that Quebec shall have 75 members and that the representation of the other provinces shall be increased accordingly, that would be an enactment quite within the authority of the dominion parliament and referable solely to the authority conferred by section 52.
I shall not read farther. One of the learned judges questioned Mr. Neweombe and asked him if it was not to apply to a certain set of circumstances, if it was not to apply to the admission of the northwest territories and Mr. Neweombe replied in the negative.
I say that if it is deemed desirable to increase the representation of Quebec, if one wants to give Quebec seventy-three members in order that it may have eight more than it has now, it is not necessary for the purpose to amend the British North America Act. Nobody has ever said that it is necessary to amend the constitution to increase the membership of the house under section 52; and we have a high authority, Mr. Neweombe, later Mr. Justice Neweombe, who says that it is not necessary. I say therefore t.o the government, by all means let us give each province full and fair representation, and that immediately. But to correct one injustice do pot initiate a second one. You may refer to the court, if you think it necessary, section 51 (4) for interpretation and you can have a decision in three weeks. If you want to go to the privy council with it you may go at the autumn session. If you wish to increase the number of members from Quebec you can bring in your legislation and this parliament has the power, so long as it preserves the parity, the proportionate representation of the provinces, to enact the means that will enable you to give Quebec more members than it has at the present time. At the same time you will, of course, have to give added representation to the other provinces.
Oh, somebody may object, you are going on with Ontario on the basis of eighty-two members. Of course you are not. You can submit that to the court, if need be. Ontario does not seek any unfair representation in this house. The unit of representation is 51,213. Divide Ontario's population by that number and it will take what comes to it without complaint.
That brings me to this point. I know that in my native province I shall be called a Tory, an imperialist, somebody who is colonially minded; I shall be called many other things. All of that does not weigh very JMr. Hackett.]

I believe it is a great misfortune that a whole ethnological group should find itself in one party. I think it is unfortunate for the party to whom that ethnological group has gone, to seek shelter, if you will. It places that party in a position of ascendancy over that element and causes it to treat it frequently shabbily and as a poor relation and as if it did not enjoy that which is essential to parliamentary government and to representative government; that is, the freedom to go elsewhere if it does not like the treatment it receives at the hands of those to whom it has given its allegiance. It is unfortunate for the party which has the entire support of any ethnological group, because it brings about that type of domination which is undesirable and *which is repugnant to the very essence of fair and representative government.
It is unfortunate for another reason. If an ethnological group gives its entire self to one party there is alwa3rs the danger and temptation that another ethnological group will range itself in opposition to it; and when a people begins to divide, not according to political conviction, but according to race, creed and other divisions of that kind, then trouble awaits that body politic.
Moreover, it is unfortunate for the group which gives itself to-I was going to say, which seeks sanctuary with-one party, because it believes that it can only find protection and self-expression within the party to which it gives its adherence. That is a misfortune, because it places that ethnological group in a position of subservience and forces it to take treatment which it could not and would not take were it entirely free.
But the misfortune does not stop there. It weighs heaviest on a party like mine which is deprived of the wisdom, the culture, the foresight and the tradition of those who make up that ethnological group. We in this party are poor, because in a crisis like this we are denied knowledge of how the heart of him who is most affected-the French Canadian- beats, what he wants, and how he would express himself were he free to break party bonds and do so.
I cannot hold myself out as the interpreter of any group. I have no title to speak for the French people. None of their blood courses through my veins. But I have the great honour-and I consider it a high honour

I want to say that if I went back to my people and had to tell them that by my vote I had consented to make their constitution, that by which they live and thrive and hope to be perpetuated, a mere statute, a mere third-rate statute such as regulates the height of a railway crossing, I would hang my head in shame and feel that I had been unfaithful to their trust in me.
When I go back to my people, regardless of what I may be called in the press, regardless of what my opponents may say of me, I want to say to them, "I believe that the constitution gave you rights and afforded you protection compared with which eight seats in any legislature-eight seats in the parliament of Canada, if you will, much as I honour the position which goes with a seat in this house- seem very small, very meagre, very mean. But when hon. gentlemen opposite accept this method of amending the constitution-and let me point out that although the constitution has been amended in the past easily and lightly, but not frequently, this is the first time that the big issue as such has ever been before parliament-this time we are taking the irretrievable step. Never again will this i parliament or anybody in it be heard to say that the constitution is a pact or a treaty. Never again, once this motion has passed, may any hon. member who votes for it raise his voice and say, "My rights have been taken from me", provided that they are taken from him at the behest of the parliament of Canada. We are at the end of a debate in which that contention must vanish forever; and the constitution of Canada will stand, when we emerge from this debate, as the merest statute which can be torn to shreds whenever the exigencies of a political party or a diminishing political majority exact it.
When we have done that, what have we from Quebec surrendered? As the constitution stands to-night, whether the population of Quebec be 100, whether it be 100,000, or whether it be 10.000,000, the province of Quebec, the minority, the people who were here first, the people who were just a little island in a whole sea of peoples of different origins, different cultures, different speech,
