The other evening the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) said that we had no reason to fear that anything would happen to the rights and prerogatives of the province of Quebec. These words are not his, but I quote them from Le Canada, the paper of his party, which gives him the following flaming headline :
La conscience universelle et le fair play britarinique protegent la langue fran<;aise.
The translation is:
The universal conscience and British fair play protect the French language.
I am going to say to the Minister of Justice that British fair play is not restricted to the British isles. I hope, I believe, I know that there is fair play not only in one but in all provinces. That being so, is there any reason why the other parties to this contract, from which the B.N.A. Act emerges, a contract the observance of which is so important and vital
to them, should not be consulted? I submit that the very essence of British fair play would impel the minister to take any amendment to this document to the provinces before going abroad with it. Is there any reason to suspect that these provinces will be unfair in considering it?
Then there is the wail that this party is in collusion with the government of the province of Quebec. So far as I am concerned I wish it were. I see no impropriety in parties finding expression both in the legislatures and in the House of Commons. I see no impropriety in closer relationship between the members of this house and the government of Quebec. Unfortunately that relationship does not exist, but in so far as I at least am concerned I would see no impropriety in such a relationship.
There is also the question which possibly I should have raised a little earlier in my remarks had I treated it in its proper place, namely, the question of cost. According to the British North America Act, 230 representatives from the various provinces of this dominion should constitute the next parliament of Canada. It will mean a reduction of twenty-five members if one considers the 255 mention pH " e motion of the minister. It is impossible iu maintain a member of parliament for less than 810,000 a year. He receives as an emolument and, for expenses, the sum of $6,000. Add to that travelling expenses; the salary of a secretary and other incidentals. I submit that the public accounts show that the cost of maintaining a member is something in excess of $10,000 a year. The sum of $10,000, multiplied by twenty-five, is $250,000, and on that basis, taking current interest rates, it entails a capital of $10,000,000, which even in these days is worth while saving.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I wish to say to the government that they have no mandate whatsoever for this proposed legislation. They should consider the time, the place and the manner in which they are asking for this legislation. The British North America Act, at the time it was passed, was looked upon as the law of the Medes and Persians; it could not be changed. You may call it a pact, a compact, a contract, an agreement or a treaty; you can call it anything you like. There is a difference of opinion on the part of those who have taken part in this debate. Some have been for one thing and some for another.
So far as this particular resolution is concerned, we have no right, for political purposes, to make a scrap of paper out of the British North America Act. That is what we are
Redistribution

doing, making a scrap of paper of the work
of the fathers of confederation. Let us look at what the government is doing to-day. If we open the door at all we shall have what happened in the United States. The house will remember what happened over there when they tried to interfere with the written constitution. There is in Canada a written constitution, the British North America Act. There is an unwritten constitution, consisting of customs, usages, conventions, precedents and all these things, which is called the unwritten law. These things have been expounded. If you open the door at all, what is to become of section 133; what is to become of section 55 of which the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) gave a learned exposition?
I can tell you what happened in the United States. They annexed ten states; some were bought from one country and some from another. In Louisiana they had a condition somewhat similar to the condition we have in one of the provinces of Canada. They had a government under Huey Long there, and look at what they did notwithstanding written law, unwritten law, the terms of a treaty and purchase or language or anything else.
The government has no mandate for this proposed legislation. Who is asking for it? Has any provincial legislature passed a resolution in favour of this legislation? I say no. I know a great many people in the province of Ontario, and I tell you the answer of this province is going to be, "No surrender." This comes at a very unfortunate time, when we consider what we have been doing since this parliament met last March. We are to have a new flag and a new anthem, and they want to abolish appeals to the privy council. I can tell you this, that the privy council is one court where a litigant can get justice. I remember a decision in 1914 of Lord Haldane, referred to by an hon. member the other evening, in connection with public ownership of light, power and transportation in the province of Ontario. We never would have had the cheap light and power had it not been for the privy council. Injunction after injunction was issued. I insisted upon an appeal to the privy council, and a great victory was won in 1912 and 1914 for municipal institutions in this province.
I am going to ask the Minister of Justice a question, because he is always polite and courteous. I want to point out that the municipalities and the provinces have a practice of submitting election matters to the people by a referendum or plebiscite. The people should vote on this resolution. Many provinces have that municipal legislation. It is a good and wise provision, because it pro-
tects the taxpayers and the voters, by a vote of the people, from what the legislatures occasionally do. I have brought into this house on other occasions a bill providing for the holding of plebiscites or referendums on these great national questions, and I should like to ask the minister if that practice could not be adopted here. After all, as has been shown in this debate, the last census was not taken properly. That was not the fault of the census officials, but resulted from the fact that the war was in progress. There *were 70,000 soldiers from the Toronto district spread all over Canada and overseas; women and war workers moved to other parts of the country, and they were not counted when the census was taken from door to door. For that reason we should wait until after the census of 1951. Then we should have a referendum or plebiscite before we change the whole system of representation which we have followed since 1867.
We would not be doing something new in holding a referendum, because late in 1941, on motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), a referendum was held in connection with changing what had been done previously in regard to one matter, and a vote was taken in every federal constituency. Here you are going to change the whole federal law and alter the present situation, which means you are going to open the door to changes in the British North America Act and make a scrap of paper out of that part of the act. The provinces exist to-day because of a treaty or agreement or contract, a pact and a compact. The provinces have their constitution under section 92; the field of federal matters is laid out in section 91. Now, over the heads of the representatives of the people, of our own accord we are going to make an application to His Majesty the King and the parliament of the United Kingdom along certain lines. I can tell you, from what has been said in the debates on the last two or three applications of this kind, that this request will not be sanctioned by the British house without a very lively debate, and questioning as to what consultation has been had with the provinces. We have been changing many things. Through isolation and separatism we have almost closed the door on the old land. Here we have a compact of 1867 upon which the two old provinces agreed, and it cannot be changed in this way.
There is another matter I should like to mention in conclusion. The first thing this house should do is recover some of the rights, privileges and functions we have lost to outside boards. Call this a free parliament! I would not call it a free parliament at all. The

press was founded on the ruins of the old type of parliamentary representation they had in England. The press has been the only organ of public opinion. The defects in our parliamentary system brought about this. From the time of the reform bill in 1834 right down to the change in the constitution which wiped out the rotten boroughs and the pocket boroughs and all that kind of thing, the press had a part to play, and they fulfilled the functions which were later performed by the House of Commons when it had real parliamentary representation. Now, if you are going to tinker with the constitution in this way you are going to cause wide disunity in this country. The people back in the constituencies must be considered. We have no mandate from them. I have no mandate from my constituents to support an, application like this; neither has any other Ontario member sitting in this house. Shades of Wallace and McCarthy and John Ross Robertson and John R. Robinson, while all this is going on in this House of Commons over the heads of the electors back home!
In my opinion the procedure is all wrong. If you make a scrap of paper out of certain sections of the British North America Act the whole thing will be wrecked, and we shall be back where we were before confederation. You will notice that no bill has been brought in with regard to this matter. In other days, when an amendment of the British North America Act was considered, the resolution was supported by a bill which had to pass both houses of parliament. I believe that should have been the practice followed here, because you cannot move the six months' hoist under this resolution. To-night I tried to introduce an amendment under which we would adopt the municipal law, but it was not even read to the house, although seconded by the hon. member for High Park. I want to point out that a private member has certain rights, privileges and functions in this house which cannot be interfered with. I remember reminding this house the other evening that when King Charles marched into parliament and addressed his honour, Speaker Lenthal, the reply was, "I have neither eyes to see nor ears to hear but as the house gives me utterance."
Once more I am going to ask the Minister of Justice, will he not agree to postpone this matter until after the census of 1951 and a referendum to the people on it? I see the minister shaking his head; apparently he is not going to answer directly. Then will he agree to adopt the municipal law? Again I see his answer is no. Well, the minister has given only
Redistribution
two noes; once in the province of Ontario we had to vote on four noes, in connection with the temperance vote. I suppose we shall just have to swallow this and say nothing more about it. If that is what parliamentary government in Canada is amounting to, the quicker the house of parliament prorogues and we have an election, the better. We shall have one in the fall anyway over this very matter of provincial and federal rights.
As I said before, the provinces are a duplicate municipal system, and they have grave questions to deal with. The British North America Act came about because of a compromise, and there should be some compromise about this matter.
I am sorry the government have taken this stand. They have no authority; they have no mandate. If the province of Ontario, which contributes about forty-one per cent of the taxes, is to have its membership cut down, then the people of Ontario will find out about it. There is no better way to wreck confederation than to pass the proposed resolution. It will not provide a system of checks and balances, or improve parliamentary representation. It is simply an application to the mother of parliaments, and I hope before long it will be thrown out over there.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, there are just a few points about which I wish to say a few words. First of all, I shall dispose of some that I had noted prior to the continuation of the debate this afternoon, and then perhaps I shall have a little to say about some of the later speeches we have heard. There seems to be some anxiety as to whether or not the enacting of the amendment proposed in this resolution would affect the provisions of the British North America Act known as section 51 (a) and section 52. Section 51 (a) reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this act a province shall always be entitled to a number of members in the House of Commons not less than the number of senators representing such province.
Section 52 reads:
The number of members of the House of Commons may be from time to time increased by the parliament of Canada, provided the proportionate representation of the provinces prescribed by this act is not thereby disturbed.
Sections 51 (a) and 52 will not be affected in any wray. It is a principle of interpretation that has even been inserted as a text in our Interpretation Act. Section 10 reads:
The law shall be considered as always speaking, and whenever any matter or thing is expressed in the present tense, the same shall be
Redistribution

applied to the circumstances as they arise, so that effect may be given to each act and every part thereof, according to its spirit, true intent and meaning.
Section 51 as proposed in this resolution; section 51 (a) as I have read it and section 52 as I have read it will still continue to speak and may, if and when occasion arises to resort to them, provide authority for whatever may be found to be the right thing to do at the proper time. The United Kingdom interpretation act, which would probably apply to this statute in view of the fact that it is a statute passed by the imperial parliament, provides in its section 8 that every secion of an act shall have effect as a substantive enactment without introductory words. Then section 32, subsection 1, provides:
Where an act passed after the commencement of this act-
That was in 1889.
-confers a power or imposes a duty, then, unless the contrary intention appears, the power may be exercised and the duty shall be performed from time to time as occasion requires.
I submit that section 51 as contained in the resolution; section 51 (a) as it already is in the act and section 52 as it already is in the act, shall all three remain there as separate enactments providing powers that may be exercised whenever occasion requires them to be used.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
May I ask the minister a question just for my own information? With respect to New Brunswick where we have ten members out of 245, if the representation is changed to ten members out of 255 would that not change the proportionate representation of New Brunswick and would that not be a violation of section 52?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Section 52 is not a section which restrains in any way the powers of the parliament of the United Kingdom; section 52 is a section which deals with the powers of the parliament of Canada. The parliament of Canada could not, by increasing the number of members of Canada, change the proportion. According to part of the argument of the hon. member for Stan-stead (Mr Hackett), with which I will deal a little later, he would seem to contend that that would be representation by population, disregarding other restrictions. But that would not be my construction. My construction of the act would be that if section 52 were used at the present time or at any time in future the number of members of parliament for a province would have to be the proportion it had prior to the increase, and if

there were an increase from 255 to 355, New Brunswick would have to have 10/255ths of 355.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Why not 10/245ths?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That is not what we are asking the imperial parliament to enact at the present time. In 1915 Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick got something which they did not have before, something which gave them representation not based upon their numerical proportion of the population of Canada. On this occasion an application is being made to get a new basis of distribution which will not reduce the representation of Prince Edward Island but which will not give it the additional half member it would receive if it were an increase made by the parliament of Canada under section 52.
I should like to call the attention of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), who was so much concerned about the vote that he did say he would give after the amendment that was then before the Chair had been defeated, to the vote and proceedings of the legislative assembly of the province of Quebec of March 7, 1945. He will find there that the following resolution was moved, seconded and voted upon after debate:
Whereas, under the amendment to the constitution in 1943 our province was deprived of its proportion of representation in ratio to the other provinces;	_
Wherefore this house invite the federal government to revise the electoral map before the elections so as to render justice to the province of Quebec.	,
That motion was put and the vote was S2 yeas, no nays. Among those who voted with the yeas was the Hon. Mr. Godbout, the same gentleman of whom the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres spoke this afternoon, and the Hon. Mr. Duplessis, of whom the hon. gentleman also spoke this afternoon. They and eighty of their colleagues in the legislature voted to invite the federal government to revise the electoral map before the elections so as to render justice to the province of Quebec. The hon. member for Stanstead has said that the party to which he belongs regards the raising of the representation of the province of Quebec to seventy-three, provided the representation of Ontario is to remain at eighty-two, as an act of justice. If that is so, if that is the view that those who are opposing this resolution take, then I can say to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres that the eighty-two members of the legislature of Quebec who voted that resolution have invited us to do that act of justice.
With respect to the legal argument advanced by the hon. member for Stanstead, with the

R edistribution
first portion of his speech I was very much impressed. I thought it was helpful, something that would be of great value to the national unity of this country. But I was unable to persist in that impression of his speech as it developed. The legal argument is that under section 52, without an amendment, if it were desired to have the representation of Quebec at seventy-three, a redistribution could be made which would give Ontario eighty-three. Let us see just what that section says.
The hon. member for Stanstead and I have grown up together. We very often have the same ideas, and this is one which I put to the law officers of the department, asking them if we could not by using section 52 bring about this fair readjustment, eliminate this overrepresentation which the province of Ontario does not want, which the members of the Progressive Conservative party, speaking through the hon. member for Stanstead, come into the house and say:	We do not want it
to continue. Nevertheless in fact we see wdiat measures are being taken to prevent the overrepresentation from being adjusted. Section 52 says:
The number of members of the House of Commons may be from time to time increased by the parliament of Canada, provided the proportionate representation of the provinces prescribed by this act is not thereby disturbed.
The opinion I got from the officers of the department was that the proportionate representation prescribed by this act was 82/245ths for Ontario at the present time and 62/245ths for Quebec at the present time, and that if there were an increase in number that would bring Quebec's up to seventy-three, then Ontario's would have to go necessarily to ninety-two, Nova Scotia to thirteen and New Brunswick to eleven, each one being increased by just a little bit less than one-eighth; Manitoba, seventeen on the basis of the last census would go from fourteen to sixteen; Saskatchewan, on the basis of the last census, would go from seventeen to nineteen; Alberta from seventeen to nineteen; British Columbia from sixteen to eighteen.
The hon. member says: Well, if you want Quebec to have seventy-three, give them seventy-three. But what difference in the proportionate representation would that make? To what degree would that cure injustice if it means adding ten to the eighty-two already representing Ontario?
The hon. member says: Well, submit it to the court. I suggested submitting it to the court, and I was told that it was quite useless to attempt to get a decision that would be anything but a strict interpretation of this
section 52, which requires the increase in number to respect the proportion of representation at the time it is made.
What objection is there to doing it in this way if it is the fair thing to do? This is a way that will do it, and do it in a manner the legality of which cannot be questioned by anyone. Nobody can pretend, if this resolution carries and an amendment is made to the British North America Act in these terms, that it will not be absolutely valid, that there can be any question whatever about its legality. Is that not the right thing to do with respect to the representation in this house? If it is the fair thing to do, why not do it in a manner about which no one can raise any question? If the hon. gentlemen on the other side agree that it is the fair thing to do, why all this debate and all this opposition and all these amendments that have been brought forward ?
But it did not stop there. I shall not impute motives; I am just drawing conclusions as to what would be the effect of the attitude, taken, and contrasting it with the speeches made from the other side in opposition to this redistribution. I am not over-impressed by the dismal picture of the future of my race in Canada drawn by the hon, member for Stanstead. I do not foresee an early day when the descendants of the French who have inhabited this country for over three centuries will be reduced to the poor fisherman washing his nets on desolate banks of the St. Lawrence. I feel that my people, those of my race, can stand on their own feet and that if they get in the parliament of their nation the right to be represented by a number of elected members proportionate to their own numbers they will be very well taken care of and they will have no occasion to complain of any unfairness. This bugaboo that is brought forth to scare them away from the restoration of something that no one here dare say is not the fair thing to do impresses me very little. Your language, it is said, will be taken from you! Your rights will be taken from you!
If this thing goes through, it will be the last of the contention that the provinces have to be consulted and then there is no protection for the rights of the minorities! If it is to be the last of the contention that the constitution of this nation cannot be amended in respect of national matters unless the proposal be subjected to the veto of the great powers who sit in the provincial capitals, then I think this is a happy day for Canada. This veto business is something which is proving very difficult in the assembly of the united nations, and if in this assembly of the repre-
Redistribution

sentatives of the Canadian people we can down it forever we shall be performing a service to the Canadian nation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
There is a problem connected with the matter of judges' pensions of which the minister is fully aware, arising out of the statute of 1944 amending the Judges Act which permitted the judges then holding a judicial office to make an election so that their pensions might be shared with their widows. The effect of the legislation was to confine it to judges then holding office, without affording any opportunity in any of its terms to permit the election to be made by any person who had at the date of the enactment of the amending act been retired as a judge. The form of the legislation was certainly not broad enough to include those persons, and if such persons, namely retired judges were to be included within the scope of such a scheme it would be necessary to introduce legislation in quite a different form, I think, because of the difference between the grant by letters patent of the pension prior to 1944 and the right to pension subsisting under the amendment of 1944. It does not

require any words from me to suggest that there was a measure of injustice to those who had been retired prior to the enactment of the amendment in 1944. It may be that there were reasons pressing on the government and parliament at the time which might have made it difficult to extend the scope of the legislation. But the principle is sound. The principle of permitting judges to make within a given period-in that case I think it was ninety days-an election to share their pensions with their widows so that in the event of their death the portion assigned to the widow could pass to her for life, was sound. I would urge that it ought to be extended to those who happened to have been retired at the date of the enactment of the amendment to the Judges Act in 1944. I am sure that the Minister of Justice must take a sympathetic view of these cases. I would ask if it is not possible for the government to indicate whether it is proper to widen the scope of the principle which received effect in the 1944 amendments? This need not be made compulsory any more than section 26A of the act as enacted in 1944. It would be purely optional to give those who are retired an opportunity, within a reasonable period, say, ninety days, to make a similar election.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: There are two matters in that connection which have been under consideration and which, I hope, will come to be dealt with before very long. One is the position of those who had retired prior to the amendment made in 1944, and who are still with us and able to make an option. The other is with respect to widows of judges, and there are several. There are a large number of judges who died before there was any section in the act permitting them to make this kind of provision. I think both will have to be considered together. I consider they are desirable things to be done, but they are not the only desirable things before the government for consideration and study, and I did not feel it would be an opportune time, at this session, to ask parliament to deal with those judges who had retired prior to 1944 and with the widows of those who had died before the 1944 statute was adopted. There were suggestions and proposals for the establishment of a system of old age pensions on a contributory basis among the things suggested to the dominion-provincial conference. Had something definite and generally satisfactory become possible as a result of that conference, I then would have felt it much easier to bring before parliament a measure to make provision for those widows and judges. I hope there will come a time, at a not too remote period,

Sup-ply-Justice
when it will be possible to consider the position of those judges who had retired and of those widows, without having to meet the criticism that there are many others just as worthy of sympathetic consideration by this parliament who should be provided for at the .same time. For that reason I felt this was not the proper time to attempt to deal with the problem referred to.
The other was dealt with in 1944 because it was an option that was granted and with respect to that it could be felt that it did not impose any serious burden on the treasury. It did not increase the amount of pension which might be payable, through two-thirds to the judge and the other one-third to his consort. It was the same amount and there were the same chances of longevity, so that it did not appear to impose any substantial burden upon the treasury. But this other provision which I should like to be able to recommend to my colleagues just as soon as we can get to it would impose quite a substantial burden upon the treasury, and I do not think it would be the kind of measure that should be recommended to this house at this session, because there are too many other things that have also to receive consideration.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Does the minister think it necessary to wait and couple those two measures together? As he has said, he extension of the option to those judges who had been retired prior to 1944 would not involve any additional burden upon the dominion treasury. Could it not then be dealt with without waiting to deal with the other question, namely pensions to judges' widows? There are some retired judges who feel-I know the right hon. gentleman is aware of this 

that an injustice had been done them in comparison with those who were on the bench when the amendment was passed in 1944. These are men who are on in years. Many of them are anxious that they should make provision for their widows by undertaking to share their pensions with them; and, since it does not involve any additional burden to the treasury, I wonder if it is not a matter that calls for early remedy.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I should not like to do that. I prefer taking them together. To do one would increase the pressure for the other. There are quite a large number of charming ladies who have been left in circumstances which make it difficult for them to provide for their requirements according to the manner in which they had lived previously; . and I think they would consider that when anything else is done about this, it should take
them in as well. I should not like to recommend doing one thing without the other. I think it would give them the impression that their case was becoming more and more remote, so that I prefer to have the two things done together. When they are done, they will take care of everything then existing. If one of the retired judges, alive to-day, should die before this is done, leaving a widow, his widow would be in the same class as the other widows to be dealt with or whose cases would come up to be dealt with.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
That would be the intention of the government if it introduced the legislation?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes. If legislation is introduced it will apply not only to widows whose husbands died in office but also to the widows of those who had been judges and had retired before their death. So that all the cases would be covered. Of course they are all anxious to have it done just as soon as possible; and the explanation I have given to large numbers of frequent, repeated representations, often from the same persons, has had to be that I did not feel I could ask parliament to deal with these cases while there were many other things that many hon. members would consider even more urgent.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
If I may say so, I think the Minister of Justice is taking the right attitude. While the question which has been asked regarding pensions to widows of judges appeals to one's sense of appreciation of the position of a judge and to the family that he leaves, nevertheless I think the minister is quite right that at this stage, when people are looking for something better in old age pensions and perhaps something in the way of a national health plan and so on, the masses of the people would expect that the government would do some of these things that have been pressed upon all of us and that many of us have warmly advocated, before singling out the dependents of a certain class of persons who during their earning years have been receiving relatively high remuneration.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
